The test is the one this whole book has pressed, now applied to the guide's own soul. The true elder is known by his transparency to Another: he points always away from himself to Christ, he labours to make the disciple free and not dependent, he decreases that the Lord may increase, and his authority is the authority of one who has himself been broken and healed and therefore wields it in fear and in tenderness. The false elder is known by the opposite marks: he draws the disciple's gaze to himself, he cultivates a dependence that flatters his own significance, he binds where Christ would loose, and he mistakes the gift of insight for a standing licence over another's life — the old confusion of the charism with the character, of gratia gratis data with holiness. The gift of reading hearts, like every charism, makes a ministry visible but does not make its holder trustworthy; only the cruciform shape of a life does that. A soul-friend or a starets who cannot be questioned has, by that very fact, ceased to be safe.

Even the Confucian world, which knew nothing of the desert, felt after this ministry of the discerning companion. Confucius counted among the three beneficial friends (益友) the friend who is upright, the friend who is sincere, and the friend of wide learning (Analects 16.4), and taught that the noble person makes friends through culture, and through friends perfects his virtue (以文會友，以友輔仁) — the recognition that even the cultivated heart cannot complete itself alone, but needs the true friend as a second eye upon the self. The parallel is real and warm: the Confucian, too, knew that self-cultivation is never solitary, and that a faithful friend discerns what the self contrives to hide. And the limit is the one that runs through the whole of this book — the Confucian friend forms the other toward the impersonal pattern of virtue, while the anamchara and the starets beget the other toward a personal Christ, by a personal Spirit whom they mediate but can never replace. Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the soul-friend and the elder are one ministry and one gift — the Spirit reading a heart through a heart that he has himself purified — and their whole authority is the authority of a window: to let the Light through, and never, for one moment, to become it.

The Chinese parallel: wandering, the empty boat, and the Way in the ten thousand things

The Celtic discernment of providence and creation finds a striking counterpart in the Daoist tradition, and the comparison illuminates both. The peregrinatio, with its holy abandonment of self-steering and its trust in a providence that carries the rudderless pilgrim, resonates with the Daoist ideal of 逍遙遊 (xiāoyáo yóu), the "free and easy wandering" of the opening chapter of the Zhuangzi, and with 無為 (wúwéi), the "non-forcing" that ceases from anxious contrivance and moves in accord with the spontaneous course of things. The Celt's coracle without oars is close kin to the Daoist image of the 虛舟 (xū zhōu), the "empty boat" that drifts with the current and, having no one at the helm, bumps against others without provoking their anger — the emblem of a self so emptied of its own willful steering that it moves in harmony with the Way. And the Celtic perception of God pervading creation resonates with the Daoist attunement to the dào present in the 萬物 (wànwù), the "ten thousand things," and with the ideal of 樸 (pǔ), the "uncarved block" of natural simplicity in which the Way is undisguised. The parallel of discipline is real and deep: both traditions teach a holy abandonment of the anxious self-will, an attunement to a reality larger than the self, and a simplicity that finds the ultimate in the ordinary and the wild.

Yet here too the parallel reaches its appointed limit, and the limit is instructive. The Daoist wanders and drifts in attunement to an impersonal Way, merging his self into the spontaneous course of nature; the Celtic pilgrim casts himself, rudderless, upon the guidance of a personal Providence who loves him and steers his coracle by a fatherly will, and who has set Christ before and behind and within him. The Daoist empties the self to accord with the Way; the Celt empties the self to be carried by the Trinity. The Daoist finds the dào in the ten thousand things; the Celt finds the Father, Son, and Spirit present in a creation that is not divine but is the sacrament of the divine presence. The discipline is parallel — abandonment, attunement, simplicity — but the object diverges, for the one lets go into an impersonal spontaneity while the other entrusts himself to a personal love; and it is the personal love, the Christian confesses, that makes the abandonment not a merging but a homecoming. The parallel, once more, illumines by both its likeness and its difference: the human heart, in Ireland as in China, learned to let go and to attune; but only where the Way is known to be a Person does the letting-go become the discernment of a providence that carries the pilgrim home.

Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the Celtic discernment of providence and creation is a vivid and precious grasp of the pneumatological — of the Spirit who fills creation and guides the wanderer, and of a discernment of God's leading that proceeds not by the anxious decoding of signs but by holy abandonment to a providence trusted. It is the desert's discernment of the will of God carried out of the cell and onto the open sea, and enlarged by the peculiarly Celtic perception that the God who is sought in the stillness of the heart is also present in the singing of the whole created world.

They set out in a boat without oars, and called it not recklessness but faith. To let God steer is the last and hardest discernment.

Weighed by the pneumatological measure

Weighed by the measure set out in the Prolegomenon, the Celtic tradition grasps the pneumatic ground with a distinctive and often-neglected vividness. Its piety is saturated with the Trinity and the Spirit — the loricae invoke the Spirit and bind the whole Trinity about the soul; its sense of God's presence pervading creation is a genuine perception of the Spirit who fills all things; its anamchara is pneumatic discernment mediated in the warmth of friendship rather than the austerity of the elder; and its peregrinatio is a discernment of providence by holy abandonment that trusts the Spirit to guide the rudderless. Being the desert transplanted to the West, it holds the desert's whole discernment — watchfulness, the manifestation of thoughts, the reading of the eight vices, the pursuit of purity of heart — in a warmer, more incarnational, and more creation-affirming key, and it adds to that inheritance the soul-friend, the medicine of souls, and the discernment of God in the wandering and in the world. Its characteristic danger, weighed honestly, is the one its penitential system would bequeath to the West — the drift toward mechanism, externalism, and the tariffing of grace, against which the Reformation would later and rightly react — together with, in its modern romanticised form, the temptation to a sentimental nature-mysticism that loosens the Trinitarian and christological anchor. But at its genuine best — in Patrick's abandonment to the God who guided him, in Columba's discernment of hearts, in Columbanus's rigour, in the soul-friendship that made the desert warm, and in the rudderless boat that trusted the winds of God — the Celtic tradition is a precious witness to the pneumatic discernment of the whole Church, and one the comfortable and disenchanted modern West has particular reason to recover.

The desert came to the West and grew warm. It kept its watchfulness, and added a friend, a boat, and the whole singing of creation.

Providence is not fate but fatherhood; and this is what makes the abandonment not resignation, but trust.

知

Part Six

The Roman Catholic Tradition

Prudence and the gift of counsel; the Ignatian art of consolation and desolation; the Carmelite mystics; and the discernment of the synodal Church.

Chapter Nineteen

Prudence, Ignatius, and the Disciplined Art of Discernment

The Roman Catholic tradition brings to the discernment of spirits two distinct and complementary geniuses, which between them constitute perhaps the most fully elaborated discernment tradition in Christendom. The first is intellectual and moral: the great scholastic theology of prudence and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, worked out above all by Thomas Aquinas, which situates discernment within a comprehensive account of the virtuous life and the perfecting of human action by grace. The second is mystical and experiential: the discernment of spirits as a practical art of the interior life, worked out above all by Ignatius of Loyola in the Spiritual Exercises, whose Rules for the Discernment of Spirits are the most precise and influential practical guide to discernment ever written. This chapter introduces both, and the chapters that complete this Part will unfold each in full, together with the Carmelite mystics who mapped the discernment of mystical experience and the modern retrieval that has carried Ignatian discernment to the whole Church and made it, in our own day, the animating principle of a synodal ecclesiology.

Prudence and the gift of counsel

For Thomas Aquinas, discernment in its ordinary form belongs to the virtue of prudence — practical wisdom, phronesis, the virtue by which reason rightly directs action toward the good in the concrete, contingent circumstances of real life. Prudence is, in the Thomistic scheme, the charioteer of the virtues, the intellectual virtue that governs the moral virtues by discerning, in each particular situation, what the good actually requires and how it is to be achieved; and it is therefore, in one aspect, discernment itself — the reasoned perception of the right course amid the ambiguities of the actual. But Aquinas knows that natural prudence, however excellent, is not sufficient for the supernatural life, and so he teaches that the Holy Spirit perfects prudence by the gift of counsel (donum consilii) — one of the seven gifts of the Spirit — by which the soul, made docile to the Spirit's own promptings, is guided in matters that exceed the reach of human reason and is enabled to discern the will of God with a certainty and a rightness that natural prudence alone could never attain. Here the Catholic tradition holds together, in a single theological structure, the two dimensions we have seen throughout: discernment as an acquired virtue, the trained practical wisdom of the mature, and discernment as a gift of grace, the Spirit's own guidance of the docile soul. The gift of counsel does not abolish prudence but perfects it; grace does not destroy nature but heals and elevates it; and the discerning Christian is one in whom a well-formed practical wisdom has become supple and responsive to the leading of the Holy Spirit.

Ignatius and the rules for discernment

If Aquinas gives discernment its theological framework, it is Ignatius of Loyola who gives it its supreme practical art. Converted from a soldier's life on a bed of convalescence, where he first learned to discern the spirits by noticing the different traces left in his soul by his worldly and his holy daydreams, Ignatius distilled his hard-won wisdom into the Spiritual Exercises, a manual for a directed retreat, at the heart of which stand two sets of Rules for the Discernment of Spirits. The genius of the Ignatian rules is that they are diagnostic and practical — not a theology of discernment but a working guide to what is actually happening in the soul and what to do about it — and that they are calibrated to the soul's condition, for Ignatius provides one set of rules for those in the earlier stages of the spiritual life, chiefly engaged in turning from sin toward God, and a second, subtler set for those who are advancing and who face the more refined deceptions of the enemy disguised as an angel of light. The whole art turns on the reading of consolation and desolation — the interior movements toward and away from God — and on a set of precise counsels for acting rightly in each. Never make a change in time of desolation, Ignatius counsels, but hold firm to the resolutions made in the preceding consolation, for the desolate soul is being ill-advised by the spirit that afflicts it; act against the desolation by intensifying prayer and penance rather than yielding to it; and in time of consolation, lay up strength and humility against the desolation that will surely come. And for the more advanced, Ignatius teaches the crucial discernment of the serpent's tail — the attention to the whole course of a train of thought, its beginning, middle, and end, so that a thought which began in apparent light but ends in disturbance, or in a subtle turning from God, is revealed by its terminus to have had an evil source, however good its beginning appeared. The Ignatian rules, together with his method for making a sound election or decision, constitute a practical science of discernment of extraordinary refinement, and they are the subject of the chapters that follow.

The seven gifts of the Spirit and knowledge by connaturality

The Thomistic account of discernment is completed by a doctrine we have so far only touched: that of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, of which the gift of counsel is but one. Aquinas teaches that the acquired and infused virtues, prudence among them, dispose the soul to act well under the ordinary direction of reason illumined by faith; but that the soul stands in need, for the perfecting of its action, of a further and higher principle — the gifts of the Spirit, by which it is made docile to the direct motion of the Holy Spirit himself, and so is enabled to act, in matters that exceed the measure of reason, under the Spirit's own promptings. Wisdom, understanding, knowledge, counsel, fortitude, piety, and the fear of the Lord are the seven, and several of them bear directly upon discernment: understanding (intellectus) gives a penetrating insight into the things of faith, a seeing into the heart of revealed truth; knowledge (scientia) gives a right judgement about created things in their relation to God, discerning the creature truly by referring it to its Creator; and counsel (consilium) perfects prudence in the particular, guiding the soul in the concrete decision by the Spirit's own light. The whole scheme places discernment, at its summit, not in the natural operation of a well-formed reason but in the soul's docile receptivity to the motion of the Spirit — and here the most scholastic of theologians arrives, by the long ladder of his distinctions, at the very height the desert reached barefoot: that discernment, at its summit, is not the achievement of a well-formed reason but the soul made docile to a motion not its own.

Aquinas adds a further refinement of great importance for our subject: the distinction between judging by reason and judging by connaturality. A man may judge rightly about the virtue of chastity, Aquinas observes, in two ways — either by the reasoned application of moral science, as the trained moral theologian judges, or by a kind of kinship or sympathy of nature with the virtue itself, as the genuinely chaste man judges, who knows the right by an inclination of his own healed nature toward it, without needing to reason it out. This knowledge by connaturality is the deepest form of discernment, for it is the perception of a soul whose own character has become attuned to the good, so that it recognises the true and recoils from the false by a trained instinct of the heart rather than by discursive proof. It is the scholastic name for what the desert called the trained sense and the connoisseur's palate, and it grounds the whole tradition's insistence that discernment cannot be separated from holiness: only the soul that has become, by grace, connatural with the things of the Spirit can discern them truly, for like is known by like, and the pure in heart alone see God.

Chapter Twenty

The First Week Rules: The Discernment of the Beginner

Ignatius of Loyola set his Rules for the Discernment of Spirits within the Spiritual Exercises, a manual not for reading but for doing — a structured retreat, made under the guidance of a director, in which the retreatant is led through the whole drama of conversion and the following of Christ. The rules come in two sets, and the genius of their arrangement is that they are calibrated to the soul's condition. The first set, appended to the First Week of the Exercises, is written for those in the earlier stages of the spiritual life — souls chiefly engaged in the purgative work of turning from sin toward God — and it addresses the relatively unsubtle warfare proper to that stage. The second set, which the following chapter will treat, is for the advancing soul and the finer deceptions it must face. To begin with the First Week rules is to begin, as Ignatius insists one must, with the elementary grammar before the advanced syntax.

The law of contrary motion

The foundational insight of the First Week rules is that the two spirits — the good and the evil — work upon the soul in contrary ways depending upon the direction in which the soul is moving, so that the very same interior sensation may have opposite sources according to the soul's condition. In those who are going from sin to sin, Ignatius observes, the enemy commonly proposes apparent pleasures, filling the imagination with sensual delights the better to hold the soul in its bondage, while the good spirit works in the contrary way, stinging and biting the conscience through the reproaches of reason. But in those who are earnestly purging their sins and advancing from good to better, the process is exactly reversed: now it is the evil spirit who harasses, saddens, and obstructs, disquieting the soul with false reasonings so as to impede its progress, while the good spirit gives courage and strength, consolations and tears, inspirations and quiet, easing the way and removing obstacles that the soul may go forward in doing good. This law of contrary motion is the first thing the beginner must learn, for without it he will misread his own interior weather — mistaking, for instance, the disquiet by which the enemy would halt his progress for the godly sorrow that first turned him from sin.

Consolation and desolation defined

Ignatius then defines, with a precision that has served the whole Church ever since, the two master-states of the interior life. Spiritual consolation he describes as every increase of faith, hope, and love, and every interior joy that draws the soul toward heavenly things and toward the tranquil peace of its Creator — the kindling of the love of God, the gift of tears that flow from sorrow for sin or from the love of Christ, and every interior movement that leaves the soul quieted and at peace in its Lord. Spiritual desolation he defines as the contrary of all this: darkness and disturbance of soul, a movement toward low and earthly things, the restlessness of various agitations and temptations that move the soul to want of confidence, so that it finds itself listless, tepid, sad, and as if separated from its Creator. The definitions are diagnostic instruments, and the whole art that follows depends upon the retreatant learning to recognise these states in himself and, crucially, to govern his response to them by rule rather than by the impulse the state itself suggests.

The counsels for desolation

The most practically valuable of all the First Week rules are those governing conduct in desolation, and their wisdom has been proved in ten thousand dark nights of ordinary Christians. The first and cardinal counsel is this: in time of desolation, never make a change, but stand firm in the resolutions and the plan of life held in the preceding consolation. For in desolation the soul is being ill-counselled by the spirit that afflicts it, and any decision made under that influence will bear the mark of its origin; the time to decide is not the time of darkness. The second counsel is to act against the desolation — not to yield to it passively but to intensify prayer, meditation, self-examination, and suitable penance, so that the soul resists rather than surrenders. And Ignatius teaches the three causes for which God permits desolation, which together form a small theology of the dark: that it may follow upon our own tepidity and negligence, and so recall us; that it may test us, proving of what mettle our love is made when its felt supports are withdrawn; and, most searchingly, that it may teach us true humility, giving us to know by experience that consolation is a gift and not a possession, that we cannot command it or manufacture it, and that all is grace. This last is a discernment of the highest order: the desolation itself, rightly received, becomes an instrument of the very humility that is the surest mark of the Spirit.

The enemy's three stratagems

Ignatius closes the First Week rules with three unforgettable images of the enemy's characteristic tactics, each carrying a counsel of resistance. The enemy behaves, first, like a bully — strong and blustering against those who yield to him, but a coward at heart who collapses before a firm and resolute face; and so the soul that stands its ground with courage finds the tempter's power to be far less than his threats. He behaves, second, like a false lover who wishes his seductions to remain secret and is undone when they are exposed — and from this comes one of the most valuable of all practical counsels, that the soul should reveal its temptations to a good confessor or spiritual director, for the enemy's suggestions draw their strength from darkness and secrecy and are very often robbed of their power in the mere disclosure, as the desert had long taught in its discipline of the manifestation of thoughts. He behaves, third, like a military commander reconnoitring a fortress, who probes the whole circuit of the walls and launches his assault at the weakest and least-guarded point — and so the soul is counselled to know its own weakest virtue and to reinforce it, expecting the attack precisely there.

Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the First Week rules are the beginner's initiation into pneumatic self-knowledge: they teach the soul to read the movements of the Spirit and of the spirits within its own interior, to distrust the counsel of its own darkness, and to submit its temptations to the light of another's discernment. Already at this elementary stage the whole logic of the tradition is present — that discernment is the perception of the source of one's inner movements, that it cannot be practised in isolation, and that its truest fruit is the humility of a soul that has learned it cannot command the grace by which alone it sees.

In the dark, change nothing. The counsel that comes in desolation bears the accent of the one who sent the dark.

Chapter Twenty-One

The Second Week Rules: The Discernment of the Advancing Soul

As the soul advances out of the purgative struggle with manifest sin into the illuminative way of a serious following of Christ, the character of the spiritual warfare changes, and with it the discernment required. The enemy, finding that he can no longer easily tempt the advancing soul to obvious evil, changes his tactics, and the coarse assaults of the First Week give way to a subtler and more dangerous deception. It is for this stage that Ignatius provides his second set of rules, which he says are more suited to those who are progressing and which address deceptions so fine that they can undo the soul precisely through its virtues. These rules are among the profoundest achievements of the whole tradition of discernment.

The angel of light

The signature deception of the Second Week is the enemy's transformation of himself into an angel of light. To the advancing soul the enemy no longer proposes evident sin, which such a soul would recognise and refuse, but suggests good and holy thoughts, apparently pious and spiritual promptings, congenial to a devout mind — and then, having gained entry under this luminous disguise, he draws the soul gradually toward his own hidden and destructive purpose. He begins by proposing what the good soul rightly desires, and ends by leading it, step by imperceptible step, into something that serves his design: an excess that wrecks the body, a subtle vanity that feeds on the soul's own progress, a scruple that poisons peace, a good pursued indiscreetly until it becomes an evil, a zeal soured into a censorious and loveless crusade. This is the deception against which the whole ascetic tradition had warned under the figure of the counterfeit light; Ignatius gives it a working method of detection.

The serpent's tail: reading the whole course

The master-rule for unmasking the angel of light is Ignatius's counsel to attend to the whole course of one's thoughts. It is proper to the good spirit, he teaches, that the beginning, the middle, and the end of a train of thought be wholly good, tending throughout to what is right; but if the course of the thoughts that a suggestion sets in motion ends in something evil, or distracting, or less good than the soul had first proposed, or if it weakens, disquiets, or disturbs the soul, destroying the peace and tranquillity it had before — this is a clear sign that the suggestion proceeded from the evil spirit, however luminous and holy its beginning appeared. The image the tradition has drawn from this is that of the serpent's tail: a thought whose head is bright and whose tail is dark, whose true nature is revealed not by its shining inception but by the poison in which it terminates. The counsel is to trace each apparently good prompting to its end, to notice where it is actually leading, and so to catch the deception by its terminus — for the enemy can counterfeit a good beginning but cannot, in the end, produce the fruit of the Spirit, and the tail always tells.

Consolation without preceding cause

Ignatius then names a single exception to the whole apparatus of suspicion, and it is of the greatest theological weight — so much so that the modern retrieval of Ignatian discernment, as we shall see, has built upon it. There is one kind of consolation, he teaches, that God alone can give, and which therefore carries its own guarantee: consolation without preceding cause — a movement of the soul wholly toward the love of its Lord that arises with no prior object, no preceding perception or act of the intellect or will to account for it, no reason that the soul can point to as its occasion. Because such a consolation has no cause within the soul's own operations, only the Creator can be its author, entering and moving the soul by his own immediate action; and this alone, of all the interior movements, the enemy cannot counterfeit, for the enemy can only work through some occasion, some object, some prior inclination, and cannot touch the soul in its naked depth without a cause. The consolation without preceding cause is thus the one place where the tradition, for all its vigilance, affirms an unmediated and self-authenticating touch of God upon the spirit — the direct self-gift of God to the soul.

The afterglow and its examination

But Ignatius immediately adds a caution of surpassing subtlety, and it is the finest point in the whole discernment of the advancing soul. Even where the consolation without preceding cause is genuine and its divine source certain, one must sharply distinguish the consolation itself from the period that follows it — the afterglow in which the soul, still warm and glowing from the divine visitation, begins to form resolutions, make plans, and frame thoughts about what it should now do. These subsequent thoughts and resolutions do not share the guaranteed character of the consolation that occasioned them; they arise from the soul's own reasoning, or may be insinuated by the good or the evil spirit, and they must therefore be carefully examined before they are trusted or acted upon. Many a soul has received a genuine touch of God and then, in the fervour of the afterglow, mistaken its own or the enemy's suggestions for a continuation of the divine leading, and so wrecked upon the rocks a voyage that God himself had launched. The counsel is to receive the consolation with gratitude but to weigh its aftermath with rigour — to distinguish the gift from the conclusions one draws about the gift.

Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the Second Week rules bring the Ignatian discernment to its summit and confirm the thesis of our study at its most delicate point. In the consolation without preceding cause, Ignatius affirms a real, immediate, pneumatic self-communication of God to the soul — a knowing that no natural cause produces and no natural faculty can reach — which is the very pattern of the pneumatic knowing of First Corinthians 2; and in the discernment of the serpent's tail and the examination of the afterglow, he provides the rigour by which that pneumatic gift is protected from the counterfeit and from the soul's own misconstruction. The pneumatic and the disciplined are not opposed but joined: the Spirit gives, and discernment guards the gift.

The head of the thought was bright; watch its tail. The enemy can counterfeit a beginning, but never the fruit.

The angel of light: the second-week deception and the serpent’s tail

Ignatius reserved his subtlest rule for the advancing soul, and it is among the sharpest instruments of discernment the tradition possesses. With beginners the enemy tempts by open evil and gross pleasure; but with those who are making progress he changes his tactics entirely and enters, as Paul warned, "as an angel of light" (2 Corinthians 11:14) — proposing not sin but a counterfeit good, a holy-seeming thought, an inspiration to greater zeal, in order to draw the soul by imperceptible degrees toward his own hidden end. Such a deception cannot be caught at its bright beginning, and Ignatius therefore teaches the discerner to attend to the whole course of the thought: to trace it from beginning through middle to end, and to watch for the point where the fair opening turns, by however slight a declension, toward disquiet, agitation, or disorder — the "serpent's tail" that betrays the serpent. The Chinese moralists named this most dangerous of counterfeits 似是而非 (sì shì ér fēi), "seeming right, yet wrong," that which wears the very appearance of the good while being its ruin. But the two detections work by opposite instruments. The Confucian holds the counterfeit up against a fixed standard and sees at a glance that it does not match. The Ignatian cannot see it at a glance at all — the false light is too like the true — and must instead follow the thought as a tracker follows a spoor, patiently, through its consolations and its desolations, until the fair path bends toward disquiet and the serpent's tail slides into view. The one measures; the other trails.

Chapter Twenty-Two

Consolation, Desolation, and the Making of a Sound Election

The Ignatian discernment of spirits is not an end in itself; it exists to serve the making of a good election — a sound choice of the state, the work, or the course of life to which God is calling the soul. The whole apparatus of the rules, the reading of consolation and desolation, the vigilance against the counterfeit, converges upon the moment of decision, and Ignatius provides, alongside the rules, a method for the election itself that has become one of the Church's great instruments of guidance. To understand the Ignatian discernment fully is to see how it issues in a discipline of decision.

Indifference: the precondition of a clear election

The precondition of every sound election, in the Ignatian scheme, is the interior freedom Ignatius calls indifference — a word that means not coldness or apathy but the opposite of disordered attachment: a soul so freed from its own cravings, so balanced before the alternatives, that it desires nothing except what better leads to the end for which it was made, the praise and service of God. Ignatius places this at the very foundation of the Exercises, in the meditation on the First Principle and Foundation, precisely because a soul that has already fixed its desire upon a particular outcome cannot discern God's will but can only rationalise its own; it will read every consolation as confirmation of what it already wants and every obstacle as a temptation to be overcome. Only the indifferent soul — genuinely open, holding the alternatives in an even balance, wanting God's will more than its own preference — is in a position to perceive that will without distortion. Indifference is thus not the absence of desire but the ordering of desire, and it is the indispensable and often the most difficult labour of the whole process, for the soul must be brought to want God's will more than it wants its own way before it can hope to discern the one from the other.

Ignatian indifference — the holy freedom that wants neither wealth nor poverty, neither honour nor dishonour, until God inclines the soul — has a striking Confucian cousin in the Analects' portrait of the noble person who, in the affairs of the world, "is neither for anything nor against anything" (無適無莫) but sides only with what is right. Both name a heart held free of every predetermined craving, poised and open, that it may incline to the good alone. The difference is the pole to which the freed heart turns — for the Confucian, righteousness; for Ignatius, the personal will of a God who is Love.

The three times of election

Ignatius distinguishes three times or occasions in which a sound election may be made. The first time is when God so moves and draws the will that the soul, without doubting or being able to doubt, follows what is shown it, as Saint Paul was drawn on the Damascus road and Saint Matthew rose from the tax-table at a word; this is the rarest and the most certain, a leading so clear that discernment has, as it were, nothing to weigh. The second time is when much light and knowledge are gained through the experience of consolations and desolations and the discernment of the different spirits — the ordinary Ignatian way, in which the soul, attending over time to the movements drawing it toward and away from a given course, and reading them by the rules, comes to perceive the direction in which the good spirit is leading. The third time is a tranquil time, when the soul is not agitated by diverse spirits and can use its natural powers freely, and must reach its decision by the disciplined use of reason under grace. The three times are not ranked as better and worse ways so much as suited to different conditions of the soul and different clarities of leading; and Ignatius's realism is shown in his provision for the third, for most decisions are made not in the lightning of the first time nor even in the rich alternations of the second, but in the level daylight of ordinary reason seeking God.

The two methods of the tranquil time

For the tranquil time Ignatius supplies two methods, and their sober practicality is characteristic. The first is the disciplined weighing of advantages and disadvantages: the soul sets the proposed course before God, lays out on either side the reasons for and against, considers them prayerfully, and chooses according to the weightier reasons — not by the pull of feeling but by the judgement of a reason seeking only God's greater service. The second method supplies a set of imaginative correctives against self-deception, three shafts of perspective that pierce the fog of self-interest: the soul is to consider what counsel it would give to a stranger it had never met who came seeking advice in the same matter, and then to take that counsel itself; to imagine itself at the hour of death, and to choose as it will then wish it had chosen; and to picture itself before the judgement seat of God, and to decide as it would wish to have decided when all is seen in that light. These devices are nothing other than instruments for restoring the indifference that self-love erodes — ways of seeing one's own situation from outside the distorting field of one's own craving — and they remain, five centuries on, among the shrewdest practical aids to honest decision that any tradition has devised.

Confirmation, and the examen as daily discernment

Having made the election by whichever way, Ignatius counsels the soul to bring it before God and to seek confirmation — to offer the decision to the Lord in prayer and to attend to whether it is met with the peace, the consolation, and the settled sense of rightness that mark the good spirit's ratification, or with a disquiet that would counsel reconsideration. And underlying the whole practice, as its daily discipline and training-ground, stands the examen — the twice-daily examination of consciousness in which the soul reviews the movements of its day, noticing where it was drawn toward God and where away, giving thanks for the former and repenting of the latter, and so keeping its interior perception exercised and awake. The examen is the ordinary school in which the extraordinary art of the election is learned; the soul that daily attends to the movements of its heart becomes, over time, fluent in the reading of them, so that when the hour of a great decision comes it is not a stranger to its own interior country. Here the Ignatian tradition offers the whole Church a discipline of astonishing practical power: the conversion of discernment from an occasional emergency into a daily habit of the attentive heart.

Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the Ignatian election shows the pneumatic knowing of the tradition issuing in the concrete guidance of a life. Indifference is the emptying of the psychikos self-will that would drown out the Spirit's voice; the reading of consolation and desolation is the perception of the Spirit's leading; and the seeking of confirmation is the humble referral of the whole matter back to the God who alone gives the increase. That Ignatius provides also for the tranquil time of reason is no betrayal of the pneumatic priority but its wise completion, for the reason of the indifferent soul, seeking only God's greater service, is itself a reason illumined and moved by grace — the mind of Christ at work in the ordinary daylight of deliberation.

Ask what you would tell a stranger. Ask what you will wish at your death. The self that answers those is nearer to God than the self that wants.

The Ignatian rules: consolation, desolation, and the counsels for the dark hour

If the desert fathers founded the discernment of thoughts and Aquinas gave it its architecture, it was Ignatius of Loyola who reduced the reading of the interior movements to a set of practical rules so exact that they remain, four centuries on, the most useful single instrument the West has produced. Appended to the Spiritual Exercises, the rules come in two sets: the first for the First Week, for souls still being purged, who are assailed by the grosser and more obvious temptations; the second for the Second Week, for those advancing, who must face the subtler deception in which evil disguises itself as good and the better becomes the enemy of the best. Both sets rest on a single discipline — the noticing of the motions of the soul, the interior stirrings the tradition had always watched — and on two master-terms around which everything turns: consolation and desolation.

Ignatius defines them with care, and the definitions are themselves a discernment. Spiritual consolation is every interior movement that inflames the soul with love of its Creator — every increase of faith, hope, and love, every drawing of the heart toward God and toward the things above; it includes the tears that spring from sorrow for sin or from the Passion of Christ or from the sheer love of God, and the quiet peace and joy that come to rest in him. Spiritual desolation is the contrary in every respect: darkness and disturbance of soul, a movement toward what is low and earthly, disquiet born of agitations and temptations, a sinking toward distrust and hopelessness and lovelessness, the soul finding itself slothful, tepid, sad, and as though severed from its Creator. And the first and most necessary discernment is that neither is to be confused with mere feeling: consolation is not the same as pleasant emotion, nor desolation the same as the natural sadness that circumstance or temperament or the body may bring; the discernment is of the direction of the movement — toward God or away from him — and not of its emotional weather. The two, moreover, have opposite authors according to the soul's own bearing: in the soul that is genuinely moving toward God, it is the good spirit that consoles and strengthens and the enemy that bites and disquiets and throws up obstacles; but in the soul that is moving away from God, the roles are exactly reversed — there the enemy soothes with false pleasures and flattering reasons, and the good spirit stings the conscience with the sharp remorse that is, in that soul, the truest mercy.

The practical heart of the rules is the counsel for the time of desolation, and here Ignatius is at his most useful. The first rule is the great one: in desolation, make no change — hold without wavering to the resolutions and decisions settled in the light of the preceding consolation, for in the dark hour our counsel is bad, and the change the desolation urges is precisely the one we must refuse, since it is the enemy, not the Spirit, who is driving it. The second is to act against the desolation: not to slacken but to intensify — more prayer, more meditation, more searching self-examination, some fitting penance — because the enemy is overcome by doing the contrary of what he suggests, and he suggests only retreat. The third is patience, holding fast in the confidence that consolation will return, and remembering that God has not abandoned the soul but withdrawn the felt consolation for its testing and its good. For Ignatius gives the reasons God permits desolation, and they are themselves a discernment of the whole spiritual life: to try us and see what we are and how far we will go for him without the wages of felt sweetness; to teach us, by its absence, that consolation is his free gift and never our possession, lest we fall into the spiritual avarice that clutches at consolations as if they were owed; and to keep us humble, knowing our own poverty. And to arm the soul, Ignatius offers three unforgettable images of the enemy. He is like a spoiled child or a weakling bully — bold and blustering the moment we give way, but a coward who flees the instant we stand firm; therefore resist, and he weakens. He is like a false lover who begs that his seductions be kept secret — his whole power depends on concealment, and his deceptions collapse the moment they are disclosed to a confessor or a discerning guide; therefore bring the temptation into the light, and it dies. And he is like a military commander who reconnoitres the fortress and attacks at its weakest and least-defended point; therefore know where your own wall is lowest, and fortify it before the assault. Resist and he flees; disclose and he collapses; guard the weak point — the tactical wisdom of the whole tradition compressed into three figures.

The Second Week rules turn to the subtler warfare, and their hinge is the finest discernment Ignatius draws: that of consolation without preceding cause. Ordinarily a consolation has a cause — some thought, some truth, some object that the mind first meets and the will then loves. But there is, Ignatius says, a consolation that comes with no preceding cause whatever — no prior perception or act to occasion it — drawing the whole soul at once into the love of God; and this, he holds, God alone can give, for only the Creator can enter and move the soul directly, without a door, and in that pure and immediate moment such consolation cannot deceive. Yet here he adds the point on which the whole later art of discernment turns: one must sharply distinguish the moment of that consolation itself from the time that follows it — the afterglow in which the soul, still warm from God's touch, begins to form its own thoughts, plans, and resolutions. These may indeed continue the movement of God; but they may also arise from the soul's own spirit, or be insinuated by the enemy trading on the lingering warmth, and they must therefore be examined with the greatest care before they are trusted or acted upon. It is precisely in that afterglow that the angel of light does his subtlest work — and to that deception the next rules, and the daily examen, are the answer. Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the Ignatian rules are the most refined Western phenomenology of the Spirit's movements against their counterfeits; and their abiding genius is that they never locate the discernment in the intensity of a feeling, but always in the direction a movement tends and the fruit it finally bears — with the standing caution, which governs the whole apparatus, that the signs reverse according to which way the soul is already facing, so that the very first question the rules put to any interior motion is the question this whole book has put to every spirit: toward God, or away?

The daily examen and the discernment of the angel of light

Two further Ignatian instruments deserve their place, for they are the practical engine and the subtlest refinement of the whole Ignatian art. The first is the examen — the examination of consciousness that Ignatius held so indispensable that he counselled its practice even when every other prayer had to be omitted. It is not, or not only, the examination of conscience that reviews the day's sins; it is the broader and gentler review of the day's interior movements — a brief discipline, made once or twice daily, of giving thanks for the day's gifts, asking the Spirit's light, walking back through the hours to notice where consolation drew the soul and where desolation or resistance pulled against it, seeking to discern in these movements the action of God and the soul's response to it, grieving what was amiss, and resolving toward the good. The examen is the daily school in which the whole capacity for discernment is trained, for it teaches the soul to notice — to become habitually aware of the interior traffic of consolation and desolation that the unexamined life lets pass unregarded — and it is by this daily noticing, far more than by any dramatic discernment in a crisis, that the Ignatian sensitivity to the movements of the spirits is slowly formed.

The second refinement is Ignatius's teaching, in the rules for the Second Week, on the deception of the angel of light — the subtlest and most dangerous of all the enemy's assaults, and the one reserved for souls making genuine progress. The beginner is tempted by what is plainly evil; but the advancing soul, who would recoil from open evil, is tempted under the appearance of good, by an enemy who, as the Apostle warns, transfigures himself into an angel of light. Such a temptation begins with thoughts genuinely holy and good, and only gradually, by imperceptible steps, deflects the soul toward the enemy's own hidden and perverse intention. Ignatius's discernment of this deception is a masterpiece of interior attention: one must trace the whole course of a train of thought — its beginning, its middle, and its end — and observe whether the entire sequence is good and leads to good, in which case it is of the good spirit; or whether, somewhere along its course, it deflects toward something less good, or unsettles the peace it began with, or draws the soul down and away toward the enemy's design. That deflection — the "serpent's tail," in the tradition's phrase, glimpsed at the end of what began as light — betrays the deceiver who entered as an angel. And Ignatius counsels the soul, once bitten, to review the whole sequence afterward, that it may learn the enemy's characteristic approach and be forearmed against its next appearance. This is the discernment of the counterfeit good, the most advanced and the most necessary of all the discernments for the soul that is truly progressing — for the further one advances, the finer and the more angelic the deceptions become.

William of St. Thierry and the Victorines: love as a way of knowing

The twelfth century deepened the discernment of the contemplative by teaching that love is itself a mode of knowledge. William of St. Thierry, in the Golden Epistle, coined the formula that would echo down the tradition — amor ipse notitia est, "love itself is a kind of knowing" — meaning that the purified soul comes to know God not by argument but by the connatural touch of a love that has been made like to its object. The Victorines gave this a structure: Hugh of St. Victor distinguished the three eyes of the soul — the eye of flesh that sees the world, the eye of reason that sees the self, and the eye of contemplation that sees God — and taught that sin had darkened the third and grace must reopen it; and Richard of St. Victor mapped the ascending degrees of contemplation with a psychologist's precision. Discernment, in this school, is the exercise of the eye of contemplation, and it is sharpened by love. The Neo-Confucians prized a kindred conviction in 體認 (tǐ rèn), a knowing-by-embodied-realisation deeper than any bookish cognition, in which the truth is grasped by being lived. But William's word cuts deeper than the sage's. The Confucian realises, by living it, a Way that was always immanent within him. William's loving-knowledge is not the realising of what he already is but communion with One who first loved him — a love poured in from outside which becomes, once received, the very eye by which its Giver is seen. The sage knows by becoming; the saint knows by being loved.

Bonaventure’s Itinerarium: the ascent of perception

The sage knows by becoming; the saint knows by being loved.

Bonaventure gathered the Franciscan and Victorine inheritance into the tradition's most perfect map of the soul's ascent, the Itinerarium Mentis in Deum, the "journey of the mind into God." The mind rises by stages of perception: it reads God first in the vestiges, the footprints of the Trinity scattered through the created world; then in the image, turning inward to find God reflected in the powers of the soul; then above itself, in the contemplation of Being and the Good; until, at the summit, understanding itself is transcended and the soul passes over into God in an excessus of love that leaves the intellect behind. The whole is a training of perception — a graded purifying and sharpening of the spiritual eye until it can bear the light. Confucius, too, taught that one rises to the highest by way of the lowest — 下學上達 (xià xué shàng dá), "learning what is below, one reaches what is above" — the ascent to Heaven made through the patient study of the near and ordinary. But the two ascents end differently, and the difference is everything. Confucius climbs, and reaches a Heaven that keeps its silence. Bonaventure climbs — and then, at the summit, the climbing stops: the intellect is left behind on the last step, and the soul is not so much lifted as seized, carried over into a God who speaks, in a love that has outrun all knowing. The one arrives by mounting; the other, by being caught up.

Gerson and the proving of spirits: a formal science of revelation

The one arrives by mounting; the other, by being caught up.

As the later Middle Ages filled with visionaries and claimed revelations, the Church felt the need of a discipline to try them, and Jean Gerson, chancellor of Paris, supplied it in his treatises On the Proving of Spirits and On the Distinction of True from False Revelations, written with the contested revelations of Bridget of Sweden in view. Gerson reduced the discernment of a claimed revelation to a set of searching questions — who receives it, what it is, why it is given, to whom the recipient submits it, and how the person lives — and set humility, obedience to the Church, and the ordinary fruits of charity above every marvel, weighing the coin of revelation as a banker weighs gold, alert to the counterfeit however bright. It is the very method Confucius prescribed for reading a person: 視其所以，觀其所由，察其所安 (shì qí suǒ yǐ, guān qí suǒ yóu, chá qí suǒ ān), "look at how a man acts, observe the springs of his conduct, examine what gives him peace — how then can he hide himself?" But they weigh different things on the one pair of scales. Confucius reads a life down to its moral springs. Gerson reads a revelation down to its source — asking not merely whether the visionary is good but whether the word is God's, testing the spirit behind the character; for the Church stands always between two abysses, and must neither quench the Spirit nor believe every spirit that flatters it with light.

The women mystics as discerners: Bridget, Catherine, Julian

The same centuries that produced Gerson's caution produced the very mystics his science was framed to try, and the greatest of them were women whose discernment outran the learning of their examiners. Bridget of Sweden submitted her revelations to the Church and saw them weighed and, after her death, defended. Catherine of Siena, unlettered yet consulted by popes, taught in her Dialogue a searching discernment of souls and of her own visions, insisting always that true revelation humbles and that the devil's counterfeit can be known by the pride and disquiet it leaves behind. Julian of Norwich, granted her sixteen "showings," subjected them to years of patient discernment, testing every consolation against the faith of the Church and refusing to trust even the sweetest sight that did not accord with it. In these women the tradition sees 大智若愚 (dà zhì ruò yú), "great wisdom appearing foolish" — a discernment deeper than the schools, borne by the unlettered and easily despised. But the sage's foolish-seeming wisdom and the mystic's are not one secret. The sage's is a subtlety he owns, held close beneath a plain exterior. The mystics' was nothing they owned at all — it came in prayer and tears, a wisdom on loan from the Spirit, and it proved its origin precisely by kneeling: for all its unschooled daring, it bowed to the Church that tried it. The hidden wisdom of the sage answers to itself; the hidden wisdom of the saint answers to Another.

Chapter Twenty-Three

The Carmelite Mystics: Teresa and John on the Discernment of Mystical Experience

If the Ignatian tradition gave the Church its practical science of the discernment of spirits in the ordinary interior life, the great Carmelite reformers of sixteenth-century Spain — Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross — gave it the profoundest discernment of mystical experience proper: the visions, locutions, raptures, and passive purifications of souls drawn into the higher reaches of contemplative prayer. Their teaching is indispensable to any complete account of discernment, for they mapped, with a psychological and spiritual acuity never surpassed, precisely the territory in which the counterfeit is most dangerous and the stakes highest — the territory where a soul that mistakes the false for the true, or clings to the true amiss, may be wrecked at the very gates of union with God.

Teresa and the discernment of visions and locutions

Teresa of Ávila, whose Interior Castle and Life chart the soul's ascent through the mansions of prayer to spiritual marriage, brought to the discernment of extraordinary experiences a shrewdness that is all the more striking for coming from one who had received such experiences in abundance. She was acutely aware of the dangers — of the deceptions of the enemy, of the tricks of a lively imagination, of the melancholy that can counterfeit spiritual states, of the vanity that mystical favours can breed — and she laid down criteria for the discernment of genuine locutions and visions that are models of sobriety. A true locution from God, she taught, is marked by its effect: it comes with a power and an authority that accomplish what they signify, leaving the soul in deep peace, quiet, and recollection; it produces humility rather than vanity, and a greater conformity to God's will; and, decisively, it never contradicts Scripture or the teaching of the Church, for the God who speaks in the soul is the God who has spoken in his Word, and does not contradict himself. The counterfeit, by contrast, leaves disquiet, or feeds self-importance, or fails to accord with the faith. Above all Teresa insisted — and this from a great mystic, not a suspicious rationalist — that all such experiences be submitted to the judgement of a learned and prudent confessor and to the teaching of the Church, and that the soul value the fruits of an experience far above the experience itself, being ready even to disregard the phenomena entirely and to hold fast only to the humility, love, and obedience they ought to produce. She would rather, she said in effect, have the virtues than the visions.

Teresa of Ávila (1515–1582), who received an abundance of visions and locutions and was schooled by hard experience in their testing, gave the tradition its most discriminating account of how to weigh them. She distinguished corporeal, imaginative, and intellectual apprehensions — the imaginative, a picture formed in the mind, being far more open to deception than the intellectual, a wordless and imageless certainty — and warned that the more sensory and spectacular the phenomenon, the more warily it must be tried. Her surest criterion was not the vividness of the experience but its effects: a locution truly from God brings peace, light, and humility, leaves the soul more obedient and more in love with God, and — her most penetrating test — the divine word effects what it says. The words are themselves the deed: when God says to the troubled soul "be not troubled," it is at once made tranquil; a locution that merely describes without accomplishing, that leaves agitation or vanity behind, is not his.

Three further marks governed her discernment. First, genuine locutions come unsought, breaking in when the soul was occupied otherwise; those manufactured by a straining imagination or an appetite for favours are suspect from the start. Second, everything must be submitted to Scripture and to a learned confessor: Teresa insisted that were a locution to contradict Scripture, she would no more heed it than if it came from the devil himself — the Word and the Church are the fixed measure against which every private word is tried. Third, she mapped the counterfeits with a clinician's eye — melancholy and a weak or overheated imagination that fabricates its own consolations; the devil's power to costume himself as an angel of light; and above all spiritual gluttony, the craving for visions and sweetness that seeks the consolations of God rather than the God of consolations.

Against all fascination with the extraordinary, Teresa set the primacy of the ordinary: the surest sign of the Spirit is not rapture but a humbled, obedient will and a growing love of neighbour — the Lord, she said, does not so much regard the greatness of our works as the love with which they are done. The visionary path is the more perilous, not the more advanced; the safest road is humility. Here Orthodox and Charismatic readers meet her and part from her: the Orthodox nepsis would share her suspicion of images and her rule of submission, while a Pentecostal reader, more hospitable to the prophetic word, would still recognise in "the words are the deed" a kinship with the testing of prophecy by its fruit and its fulfilment. The Confucian tradition too distrusted the showy and prized the substantial — Confucius's warning that 巧言令色，鮮矣仁 (qiǎo yán lìng sè, xiǎn yǐ rén), "clever words and an ingratiating manner are seldom found together with true virtue" (Analects 1.3): the glittering surface is precisely what the discerner must see past. Yet Teresa's measure is finally not moral sincerity alone but the peace that only the personal God can effect in the soul he addresses.

John of the Cross: the counsel of detachment

John of the Cross, Teresa's collaborator in the Carmelite reform and the supreme poet-theologian of the mystical ascent, carried the discernment of extraordinary experience to its most radical conclusion. His counsel, worked out in the Ascent of Mount Carmel, is startling and bracing: the soul is not to seek, desire, or cling to supernatural apprehensions — visions, locutions, revelations, spiritual feelings — even when they are genuinely from God, but is to pass beyond them all, in the naked darkness of faith, to God himself. For faith, John teaches, is the proximate means of union with God, and God as he is in himself infinitely exceeds every particular apprehension the soul can grasp; to cling to any vision, however genuine, is to halt at a signpost instead of continuing to the destination, to prefer a created gift to the uncreated Giver, and to expose oneself to grave dangers — for attachment to spiritual experiences breeds pride, opens the door to the enemy's counterfeits, and arrests the soul's progress into the pure faith that alone unites it to God. John does not deny that God gives such graces or that they may do good; he insists that the mature soul receive them, if they come, with detachment and without clinging, and never make them the object of its desire or the measure of its progress. This is a discernment of the highest order, for it relativises the whole realm of the extraordinary in the name of the God who is beyond it, and it provides the surest of all protections against prelest: the soul that desires nothing but God in naked faith cannot be seduced by a counterfeit light, for it is not seeking light at all, but God in the darkness.

John's counsel of detachment — the nada, nada, nada by which the soul is stripped of every grasping attachment that it may be filled with God — has its unmistakable analogue in the Daoist 無為 and the return to the 樸, the uncarved block: the letting-go of the self's grasping so that a truer action, not one's own, may arise. Both know that the clutching self distorts all it touches, and that only the unclenched hand can receive. And both are parted at the root by the End of the emptying — for John empties the soul not into an impersonal spontaneity but into union with the living God who is its All.

The discernment of the dark night

John's most precious contribution to our subject is his discernment of the dark night — the passive purifications by which God himself, and not the soul's own effort, purges the senses and then the spirit, drawing the soul from meditation into contemplation and from its own activity into a receptive stillness before God. The night is a work of grace, but it is experienced as darkness, aridity, and the loss of all felt consolation, and it can therefore be catastrophically misread — mistaken for tepidity, for sin, for the withdrawal of God, or, in our own age, for mere depression — with the result that souls abandon the very path God is opening before them, or torment themselves with a false guilt, precisely when they are being led most deeply. John therefore supplies signs by which the genuine contemplative night is discerned from mere lukewarmness or melancholy: that the soul finds no consolation either in God or in creatures, so that the dryness is not the pull of some rival pleasure; that it is anxiously concerned that it is not serving God, and turns to him with painful solicitude, so that the aridity is not the carelessness of tepidity; and that it can no longer meditate discursively as before, its former methods of prayer having gone dry, while it is drawn toward a simple, loving, general attentiveness to God. Where these signs concur, the darkness is not the absence of God but the too-great nearness of a God whose light is, to the yet-unpurified soul, a darkness; and the counsel is not to strive to recover the old consolations but to rest in faith and loving attentiveness, allowing God to do his purifying work. That this discernment bears directly upon the modern pastoral question of the relation between the dark night and clinical depression is a matter to which we shall return in the concluding Part; here it is enough to mark the Carmelite gift of a discernment fine enough to distinguish the purifying darkness of God from the darkness of sickness and of sin.

Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the Carmelites offer the tradition its most exalted confirmation of the pneumatic priority and its most radical safeguard. John's counsel of detachment is the practical form of the truth that God infinitely exceeds every created apprehension and is known, at the last, not by any phenomenon the natural faculties can grasp but by the naked faith that is the Spirit's own gift; and his discernment of the night is the reading of a purely pneumatic work of God that the natural understanding, left to itself, would entirely misconstrue. Here the psychikos would see only darkness, sickness, or the absence of God; the pneumatikos, taught by John, discerns the hidden hand of a purifying grace. The Carmelite science is, in the end, the discernment of a God who is beyond being, met in a darkness brighter than all light.

Do not cling to the vision; the vision is a signpost, and you were made for the country it points to. Pass on, in the dark, to God.

Chapter Twenty-Four

From Francis de Sales to the Synodal Church

The Roman Catholic discernment tradition did not end with the great mystics; it flowed on, gentled and democratised by Francis de Sales for the ordinary Christian in the world, retrieved and deepened by Karl Rahner for the modern theological mind, and enlarged in our own day into a principle of the Church's communal life under the name of synodality. This closing chapter of our Roman Catholic Part traces that flowing-on, and shows how the discernment of the individual soul becomes, at the last, the discernment of the whole gathered Church.

Francis de Sales: discernment for the world

Francis de Sales, the gentle bishop of Geneva, took the discernment tradition — much of it monastic and mystical in origin — and made it the possession of the layperson living an ordinary life in the world. His Introduction to the Devout Life and his great Treatise on the Love of God teach a discernment marked above all by gentleness: a wariness of the anxious, scrupulous, self-tormenting spirit that mistakes agitation for conscientiousness, and a confidence that God leads the willing soul with a fatherly patience. De Sales distinguishes the signified will of God — made known in the commandments, the counsels, the duties of one's state, and the inspirations of grace — from the will of God's good pleasure, which is disclosed in the events and circumstances that befall us and is to be met with a loving acceptance; and he teaches a holy indifference that, echoing Ignatius, holds the soul open to whatever God wills. For the discernment of inspirations he gives criteria of characteristic mildness and shrewdness: a true inspiration leads to greater humility, charity, and obedience, and leaves the soul in peace; the false is known by the disquiet, the pride, or the disobedience to which it tends; and the surest safeguard, for layperson as for religious, is to submit one's inspirations to a wise spiritual director rather than to trust one's own judgement in one's own case. De Sales's enduring gift is to have shown that the whole science of discernment is not the preserve of cloistered contemplatives but the birthright of the butcher, the baker, the magistrate, and the mother — a discipline for the kitchen and the counting-house as much as for the cell.

Rahner and the existential logic of discernment

In the twentieth century Karl Rahner returned to the Ignatian rules with the eye of a systematic theologian and drew from them a significance that Ignatius had practised but not theorised. Fastening upon the consolation without preceding cause, Rahner argued that it names the point at which the human spirit experiences the immediate self-communication of God — the direct, unmediated touch of grace upon the depths of the person, prior to and beneath every particular concept or object — and that this experience is the ground of a genuinely existential discernment: a knowing of God's concrete will for this individual person in this unrepeatable situation, which is not merely the application of universal moral norms to a particular case but a real perception, in the light of grace, of the singular thing God is calling this soul to be and do. Rahner saw that Ignatian discernment presupposes that God deals with the individual immediately, that there is a divine leading of the concrete person that exceeds what can be deduced from general principles, and that the discernment of spirits is the way this leading is perceived. In arguing so, Rahner made explicit the pneumatological foundation of the whole tradition: that beneath every rule and every criterion lies the immediate self-gift of the Spirit to the human spirit, and that discernment is finally the reception of that gift. His retrieval stands as one of the clearest modern statements of the thesis of this book — that pneumatology precedes ontology, that the immediate experience of the Spirit is the ground of the true knowledge of God's will, and that discernment is the pneumatic perception of the concrete.

Communal and synodal discernment

Finally, the Ignatian tradition has always known that discernment is not only individual but communal, and this dimension has come, in the contemporary Roman Catholic Church, to a new prominence. Ignatius and his first companions, in the Deliberation of the First Fathers of 1539, faced together the momentous question whether to bind themselves into a single body under obedience, and they resolved it not by the decree of a leader but by a shared process of prayer, the laying-out of reasons on every side, and the patient seeking of the movement of the Spirit among them — a model of communal discernment that the Society of Jesus has practised ever since. In our own day this Ignatian inheritance has flowed into the wider Church under the name of synodality: the conviction that the whole Church, at every level, is called to discern together the leading of the Spirit, listening to one another and to the sensus fidei of the faithful, in a common seeking of God's will. The promise of this recovery is great — a Church that discerns together, as the Jerusalem Council did, and can say again "it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us." Its perils are equally real, and honesty requires that they be named: that the language of discernment can be misused to relativise the settled teaching of Scripture and the tradition, to baptise a predetermined conclusion, or to substitute the spirit of the age for the Spirit of God. The tradition's own safeguards answer these perils — the anchoring of all communal discernment in the Word, the rule of faith, and the communion of the Church, and the testing of every claimed leading of the Spirit by the criteria this whole book has traced. Where those safeguards hold, synodal discernment is the maturing of the individual gift into the discernment of the Body; where they fail, it becomes the very counterfeit against which the whole tradition warns. Which it proves to be, in any given instance, is itself a matter for discernment.

Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the Roman Catholic tradition, taken whole, is the Church's most fully elaborated science of pneumatic discernment — from the beginner's rules to the mystic's dark night, from the individual election to the synod of the whole Church. Its standing temptation, named already in its portal chapter, is to let the pneumatic be subordinated to a natural scaffolding of prudence or procedure; its glory, in Ignatius and the Carmelites and Rahner and the best of the synodal vision, is to have shown that beneath every rule lies the immediate self-gift of the Spirit, and that all the elaborate machinery of discernment exists only to receive, protect, and obey that gift.

The rules are scaffolding. The building is the touch of the Spirit upon the soul — and scaffolding that forgets the building is only a cage of poles.

John of the Cross (1542–1591) gave discernment its most searching account of attachment — for the peril he named is not gross sin but the soul's clinging (apego) to anything less than God, and especially its clinging to spiritual consolations and even to visions and locutions themselves. His counsel was nada: to reach union with the God who lies beyond every image and apprehension, the soul must pass through a self-emptying of all its particular graspings — to come to possess all, he taught, desire the possession of nothing. The Daoist sages charted a strikingly parallel via negativa in 為道日損 (wéi dào rì sǔn), "in the pursuit of the Way one decreases daily" — decreasing and again decreasing until one reaches non-action (Daodejing 48), the way of subtraction set against the way of accumulation. The formal parallel is exact and profound; but the divergence is the whole matter: the Daoist decrease empties toward the impersonal Way and non-action, while John's nada empties the soul only to be filled — by todo, the All, which is God himself — so that its darkness is dark not from vacancy but from an excess of light, and its dispossession is for the sake of a personal union of love.

John's most precious gift to the discernment of spirits is his rule for distinguishing the passive night of sense — God's own weaning of the soul from discursive meditation into the obscure, loving, general attentiveness of contemplation — from mere lukewarmness, distraction, or melancholy. He gave three signs that must occur together. First, the soul finds no consolation either in the things of God or in creatures; for were the dryness born of tepidity or sin, the appetite would still stray to creaturely comforts, and its finding no rest anywhere marks instead the hand of God. Second, the soul is beset by a painful, anxious carefulness that it is not serving God, a fear that it has slipped backward — and this very solicitude, John saw, is itself proof that the dryness is not negligence, since the negligent do not grieve. Third, the soul can no longer meditate or work with the imagination as before, however it strains, and is drawn instead toward a quiet and loving gaze. Where these three concur, the darkness is grace, and the soul must cease its striving to meditate and rest in the loving awareness God is giving.

This yields one of pastoral theology's most needful discernments: the difference between the dark night and depression. John himself distinguished the divine night from the humor melancólico, the melancholic humour, and the differential he implies is precise. The passive night draws the soul, even amid its dryness, toward God in a secret peace and a deepening humility and love; clinical depression, by contrast, tends toward a pervasive loss of function, toward self-hatred rather than humility, and toward a flattening that touches the whole of life and not the spiritual appetites alone — and it asks not for spiritual counsel only but for the care of the whole person. To romanticise depression as "the dark night," or to spiritualise away a treatable illness, is a grave failure of discernment; so too is the opposite error, of reducing every genuine night of grace to pathology. Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the Carmelites complete the Catholic contribution: Teresa teaching the soul to test the word by the peace it effects, and John teaching it to read even its own darkness — to know when the absence of consolation is not the withdrawal of the Spirit but the Spirit's own deeper and more hidden work.

The Thomist synthesis I: prudence perfected by the gift of counsel

The Roman Catholic tradition's most systematic account of discernment is the Thomist, and it begins with the virtue of prudence (prudentia) — the perfected practical reason that discerns, in the concrete and unrepeatable case, what is truly to be done. Prudence is not cleverness, nor mere caution, but the crown of the moral virtues, the charioteer that guides them all; and its work is precisely discernment — the reading of the particular situation in the light of the true end, and the choosing of the fitting means. Aquinas analyses it with great care into its parts — memory of the past, understanding of the present, docility to the wise, sagacity, reasoning, foresight, circumspection, and caution — a whole anatomy of the discerning judgement that no later psychology has bettered.

But Aquinas saw, with characteristic honesty, that prudence alone is not enough for the Christian life — for the human reason, however well-formed, cannot reach to the singular providence of God, nor keep the soul steady amid the infinite contingencies through which the Spirit leads. And so, above the acquired virtue of prudence, he set the infused gift of counsel (donum consilii), one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: a supernatural docility by which the soul is made pliable to the direct motion of the Spirit, moved and guided by God in the particular case beyond what its own prudence could discern. Here the Thomist account meets the whole burden of this book: natural prudence is real and necessary, but discernment in its fullness is the dianoia of a well-formed reason taken up, illumined, and moved by the nous under the Spirit — the human faculty perfected by a divine gift. The Confucian tradition reached, from its own side, toward this crown of practical wisdom in the ideal of 時中, the "timely mean" that hits the fitting thing in each moment, and in the discretionary weighing of 權; but where the sage attains the fitting by a cultivated moral sense, the Christian receives it, at the last, by a docility to the personal Spirit who counsels from within.

The genius of the Thomist synthesis is thus its refusal of two opposite errors. It will not reduce discernment to a technique of the natural reason, as though a keen enough prudence could do without grace; and it will not dissolve it into a mysticism that despises the reason and waits only for promptings, as though the gift of counsel bypassed the formed and virtuous mind. Rather, grace perfects nature: the gift of counsel does not replace prudence but crowns it, moving a reason already made wise by virtue — so that the discerning Christian is neither the mere technician of casuistry nor the passive enthusiast of impressions, but a soul whose well-formed practical wisdom has become supple to the Spirit's own guidance, reason and gift, nature and grace, working as one.

The Thomist synthesis II: knowledge by connaturality and the seven gifts

Beneath the gift of counsel lies the mode of knowing proper to all the gifts, which Aquinas names knowledge by connaturality — the knowing not by study but by kinship, in which one judges rightly of a thing because one has become akin to it.
