Confucius had reached the same bar of judgement in the discernment of persons: once deceived by fine words, he resolved, he said, henceforth 聽其言而觀其行 (tīng qí yán ér guān qí xíng), "to hear their words and observe their conduct" (Analects 5.10) — for the deed, not the profession, reveals the person. Weighed by the pneumatological measure, Edwards gives the Protestant tradition its most exacting instrument: the discernment of the Spirit not in the fire of the experience but in the fruit of the transformed and practising life.

The Chinese parallel: the classic, the illumined heart, and the new sense

The Protestant reframing of discernment around the Word finds a genuine, if unexpected, counterpart in the Confucian reverence for the jīng (經), the canonical classics, as the objective standard against which the heart-mind is to be disciplined and its every prompting tried. And the great internal debate of the Neo-Confucian tradition — whether the classics are grasped by the investigation of things through the texts, as Zhu Xi taught, or by the extension of the innate knowing from within, as Wang Yangming countered — is a remarkably close structural parallel to the Protestant question of Word and Spirit: whether the objective canon is primary and the heart is formed by submission to it, or whether the illumined heart is the seat of a knowing that the canon only awakens. The Reformed insistence that the Word is rightly perceived only through the inner witness of the Spirit, and Calvin's image of Scripture as the spectacles through which alone the bleary-eyed heart sees, correspond to the Neo-Confucian conviction that the classics yield their meaning only to a rectified heart-mind and remain a dead letter to an unpurified one.

The sharpest and most illuminating parallel of the entire comparison, however, is between Jonathan Edwards and Wang Yangming, and it is a parallel that turns, at its very centre, into the decisive divergence. Edwards taught that the regenerate perceive divine things by a new spiritual sense, a Spirit-given faculty of perception that the natural person wholly lacks; Wang Yangming taught that every person possesses the liángzhī, an innate and luminous moral knowing that needs only to be cleared of obstruction to shine forth. The two doctrines are formally almost identical — a luminous inner faculty of spiritual discernment, obscured in the unregenerate and radiant in the cultivated — and yet they divide precisely on the question of nature and grace that is the very heart of the Reformation. For Wang, the light is innate, the native possession of the heart-mind, requiring only to be uncovered; for Edwards, the new sense is not native at all but supernatural, a gift bestowed in regeneration, wholly from without, a new foundation of perception that the fallen self could never uncover because it does not possess it. Here the Chinese parallel serves the Christian argument at its most exacting, for it sets the two answers side by side in their sharpest form: the discerning light is either the flowering of the self or the gift of the Spirit — and the whole of this book contends for the second.

Weighed by the pneumatological measure

Weighed by the measure, the Protestant traditions grasp the pneumatic priority in a form that is easily overlooked because it is stated in the idiom of the Word rather than of the nous. Calvin's doctrine of the noetic effects of sin — that the natural mind is darkened and cannot receive the things of God — is precisely the psychikos of First Corinthians 2, and his insistence that only the inner witness of the Spirit gives true perception is a pneumatic epistemology in Reformed dress; Luther's theology of the cross, which finds God hidden under the opposite of what natural reason expects, is a surpassing of natural ontology by the Spirit's hidden work; and Edwards's teaching that the regenerate perceive by a new spiritual sense — a Spirit-given faculty the natural person wholly lacks — is perhaps the closest any Western tradition comes to a direct exposition of the pneumatic knowing of First Corinthians 2. The genus is grasped. The characteristic danger lies at the species: where the tethering of the Spirit to the Word hardens into a cessationism that denies the Spirit's present-tense speech, the tradition loses the living charism the same Scripture commends, and under-realises in practice the very pneumatic freedom its own epistemology affirms.

The Religious Affections: Edwards’s anatomy of the gracious heart

Jonathan Edwards's Treatise Concerning Religious Affections is the most searching analysis of the discernment of a true work of grace the Protestant tradition has produced, born of the need to distinguish, amid the fervours of the Great Awakening, the genuine from the counterfeit. Edwards argues that true religion consists in great measure in holy affections — that a heart truly touched by God is moved, and not merely informed — but then, with unequalled rigour, he strips away the unreliable signs: intensity of feeling, bodily effects, fluency in religious talk, the order of one's experiences, even a great confidence of one's own state prove nothing, for the counterfeit can produce them all. The one sure sign, he concludes, is Christian practice, the fruit borne out in a changed life; and beneath the affections he locates a "new spiritual sense," a relish for the beauty of holiness itself, given only in regeneration. Confucius mapped the same ascent from notion to delight — 知之者不如好之者 (zhī zhī zhě bù rú hào zhī zhě), "to know it is not as good as to love it, and to love it not as good as to delight in it" — and Mencius named a force 沛然莫之能禦 (pèi rán mò zhī néng yù), "so overflowing that nothing can withstand it." But the two delights are not one relish: Confucius's delight is a refinement of the natural man, and Mencius's flood the welling-up of a cultivated nature, while Edwards's new sense is a taste imparted by the Spirit in the new birth, of which the natural man, however learned or earnest, has simply no organ.

The natural man may know every doctrine of grace, and have no taste of the sweetness of the God they describe.

Rightly dividing: the Marrow and the discernment of law and gospel

The Reformation bequeathed one further instrument of discernment so basic that its neglect deranges all the rest: the distinction of law and gospel. The eighteenth-century Marrow controversy in Scotland, in which Thomas Boston and the Erskines defended The Marrow of Modern Divinity against the charge of antinomianism, turned on precisely this — the discernment of when to speak the word that kills, the law that slays presumption and drives the self-righteous to despair, and when to speak the word that makes alive, the free gospel that raises the despairing sinner by grace. To confuse them is fatal in both directions: legalism preaches gospel-duties as law and crushes the tender; antinomianism preaches licence as gospel and flatters the presumptuous. The art is that of "rightly dividing the word of truth" (2 Timothy 2.15), and Zhuangzi's parable of 庖丁解牛 (páo dīng jiě niú), Cook Ding carving the ox along its natural seams so that his blade never dulls, is its perfect natural image — the cut that follows the true grain rather than hacking across it. Yet the divergence remains: Cook Ding follows the impersonal grain of the Way by a mastery long acquired, while the preacher divides law from gospel by the Spirit's light upon the Word — a discernment given rather than mastered, whose end is not effortless skill but the freeing of a bound conscience by grace.

Rightly divided, the same Scripture kills and makes alive: the law to slay presumption, the gospel to raise the slain.

The state of a soul is discerned not in solitary introspection, where self-deception thrives, but in the loving scrutiny of friends, where it can hardly survive.

The Anglican way: discernment and the threefold cord

Among the churches of the Reformation, Anglicanism holds a place peculiarly its own — neither simply Protestant nor Roman, but a reformed catholicism, a settlement that sought the via media, the middle way, between Geneva and Rome. Its genius has been comprehension: the holding-together within one communion of the catholic and the reformed, and in later centuries the evangelical and the charismatic besides. And its manner of discerning spirits is correspondingly its own — resting neither on the single authority of an infallible Church nor on the bare letter of an unaided Bible, but on what its divines came to call a threefold cord: Scripture, reason, and tradition, bound together and not easily broken, with Holy Scripture supreme among the three.

The classic articulation is Richard Hooker's, in the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity, written against the Puritans on the one hand and Rome on the other. Scripture, Hooker taught, is supreme and perfectly sufficient for all things necessary to salvation; but reason — the light of understanding that God himself has kindled in us — and the tradition and authority of the Church have each their proper and subordinate place beneath it. For the discernment of spirits this settlement has real force: the inner light and the private judgment are never left to themselves, but are tried against the public Scripture, the reason of the whole, and the mind of the Church gathered across the centuries. It is a double bulwark — against the tyranny of a magisterium that would bind the conscience beyond the Word, and against the anarchy of the enthusiast who makes his own impression the measure of all things. The Anglican instinct, at its soundest, is a deep distrust of the unmoored private revelation, and a matching insistence that the spirit be tested in the company of Scripture, reason, and the communion of saints.

The Anglican tries the inner light not against an infallible Church nor a bare Bible, but against a threefold cord — Scripture supreme, with reason and the communion of saints.

The cure of souls: the pastoral and mystical stream

Alongside this ran a rich tradition of the cure of souls and of spiritual direction, quieter than the Puritan casuistry but no less searching. The Caroline divines gave Anglican discernment its pastoral temper — Lancelot Andrewes at his private prayers, George Herbert's country parson, Jeremy Taylor's Holy Living and Holy Dying — unspectacular, wise, and formed by the Prayer Book and the Church's year. The Oxford Movement recovered the practice of sacramental confession and direction; and in the twentieth century the stream ran full again in Evelyn Underhill and the retreat movement, in Martin Thornton's pastoral theology, and in Kenneth Leech, whose Soul Friend retrieved for Anglicans the very anam chara tradition this book has honoured. Here discernment is the patient and humble labour of the soul-friend and the director — itself a middle way, steering between the excesses of a raw enthusiasm and the deadness of a mere formalism, and trusting that the Spirit forms souls slowly, through Word and sacrament and the long companionship of the wise.

The evangelical and the charismatic streams

Two further streams meet in the Anglican discernment of the modern age, and their meeting is itself instructive. The evangelical Anglicans — Charles Simeon in his Cambridge pulpit, J. C. Ryle with his plain vigour, and in our own time John Stott and J. I. Packer — pressed a sober, word-centred account of guidance and discernment: the mind renewed by Scripture rather than swayed by inner impressions, a steady suspicion of the merely subjective, a conviction that the will of God is found chiefly in the Word obeyed and the mind sanctified. And then, astonishingly, the charismatic renewal swept through Anglicanism from the nineteen-sixties: Michael Harper and the Fountain Trust, David Watson's union of evangelism and renewal at York, Michael Green's apologetic warmth, and later the deep influence of John Wimber and the Vineyard upon a generation of Anglican evangelicals — David Pytches, the New Wine movement, the recovery of words of knowledge, of healing, and of prophecy within the ordinary life of the parish. A living deliverance ministry grew up beside it, worked at soberly by practitioners in the field rather than pronounced upon from above. The remarkable thing is that Anglicanism held these together — the cautious, word-centred discernment of its evangelicals and the open expectancy of its charismatics — in one uneasy but real communion; and that holding-together is itself a work of discernment, the refusal to let the sober quench the fire, or the fire despise the sober.

The doctrine of the mean, and the peril of the middle way

The Anglican via media, and the comprehension it seeks, find a natural mirror in the Confucian 中庸, the doctrine of the mean — which is no bland compromise but the unwavering equilibrium that holds the centre under every pressure — and in Confucius's 和而不同, harmony without uniformity, the concord of genuinely different voices that is the very ideal of Anglican comprehension. Yet the mirror shows a divergence as well as a likeness. For the Confucian mean is a balance the cultivated self achieves within an impersonal cosmic order; whereas the Anglican comprehension, at its best, is not a balance the Church strikes by its own moderation but a unity the Spirit gives — holding real and costly differences together in the one Body of a personal Lord.

And here the tradition's peculiar peril must be named alongside its gift. The middle way can curdle into mere moderation; comprehension can decay into indifference; and the threefold cord, meant to bind the inner light fast to the Word, can be loosened into a discernment reduced to reasonableness, to good taste, and to the avoidance of extremes — a cool and temperate religion that has quietly discerned away the fire, and mistaken an English moderation for the peace of God. The besetting temptation of the middle way is a reasonableness that quenches the Spirit in the name of balance. The remedy is the tradition's own best self: the threefold cord held not as a formula of compromise but as three servants of the one Word; and comprehension held not as indifference but as love — the Spirit's own gift of bearing the difficult together for the sake of Christ, in a communion wide enough to make room for the fire and grounded enough to test it.

The via media can curdle into mere moderation — a discernment reduced to reasonableness, that quenches the Spirit in the name of balance.

Comprehension, at its best, is not a balance the Church strikes, but a unity the Spirit gives.

靈

Part Eight

The Evangelical Tradition

The Berean conscience — the sufficiency of Scripture, the renewed mind, and the long debate over guidance and the will of God.

Chapter Thirty

Scripture, the Renewed Mind, and the Will of God

The Evangelical tradition inherits and intensifies the Reformation's central conviction — the supreme authority and sufficiency of Scripture — and makes it the animating principle of its whole approach to discernment. For the Evangelical, the paradigmatic act of discernment is the testing of every teaching, every spirit, every claimed leading, and every experience against the plain teaching of the written Word of God, which is the final and sufficient norm for faith and life. The pattern is the noble Bereans of the Book of Acts, who received the word with all readiness of mind and yet searched the Scriptures daily to see whether the things preached to them — even by the apostle Paul himself — were so; and this Berean posture, at once open and testing, receptive and critical, is the essence of Evangelical discernment. It produces a tradition marked by a vigilant concern for sound doctrine, a readiness to test teachers and teachings against Scripture, a suspicion of any appeal to private revelation or spiritual experience that would claim an authority alongside or above the Word, and a deep confidence that God has spoken sufficiently in Scripture for all that pertains to life and godliness. This chapter introduces the Evangelical discernment and its characteristic concerns, and the chapters that complete this Part will unfold them: the testing of truth by Scripture, the theology of the renewed mind and the illumination of the Spirit, the long and instructive debate over guidance and the will of God, and the balance the tradition seeks between credulity and a censorious spirit.

The renewed mind and the illumination of the Spirit

Evangelical discernment is not mere rationalism, the cold application of a text, for the tradition knows well that Scripture is rightly understood only by a mind renewed and illumined by the Spirit. It takes with full seriousness the noetic effects of sin — the corruption of the understanding itself by the Fall, so that the natural mind is not a neutral instrument but a darkened one, prone to suppress the truth and to rationalise its own desires — and it insists therefore that genuine discernment requires the renewing of the mind of which Paul speaks, the transformation by which the believer is enabled to prove and approve the will of God, and the illumination of the Spirit, by which the same Spirit who inspired the Word opens the believer's understanding to receive it. The Evangelical thus holds together the objective norm and the subjective condition: the Word is the standard, but only the renewed and Spirit-illumined mind can rightly apply it, and discernment is therefore both a matter of knowing the Scripture and a matter of being transformed by grace into the kind of person who can perceive its bearing on the concrete case. This is why the tradition joins to its emphasis on doctrine an emphasis on sanctification, on the cultivation of a mind and heart conformed to Christ, as the personal precondition of sound discernment.

The great debate: guidance and the will of God

The most distinctive and instructive feature of Evangelical discernment is its long and vigorous debate over the question of guidance — how the individual believer is to discern the will of God for the concrete decisions of life. Two broad positions have contended, and the debate between them is genuinely illuminating for the whole Church. The first, which may be called the traditional or specific-will view, holds that God has an individual, detailed plan for each believer's life — a specific will regarding vocation, marriage, location, and the rest — which the believer is responsible to discover, and which God makes known through a combination of Scripture, prayer, the inner witness or "peace" of the Spirit, the counsel of others, the arrangement of circumstances ("open" and "closed" doors), and sometimes more direct impressions or promptings. On this view, discernment of guidance is largely the reading of these various indicators to discover the pre-existing divine blueprint. The second, which may be called the wisdom view and which has been powerfully argued by such writers as Garry Friesen in Decision Making and the Will of God and Bruce Waltke in Finding the Will of God: A Pagan Notion?, holds that this quest for a hidden individual blueprint is both unbiblical and spiritually harmful — that God's revealed moral will, made known fully in Scripture, is the proper object of the believer's obedience, and that within the wide bounds of that moral will the believer is set free to choose, using sanctified wisdom — the counsel of Scripture's principles, prayer, godly advice, sober assessment of circumstances, and the freedom of a mind conformed to Christ — without the anxious and often superstitious hunt for signs and impressions that the specific-will view can encourage. The wisdom view warns that the quest for a detailed hidden will breeds paralysis, superstition, and a kind of spiritualised fortune-telling, and that it can even become an evasion of the responsible freedom and maturity to which God calls his children.

The debate is not merely a family quarrel; it goes to the heart of what discernment of guidance is, and the mature Evangelical position — represented by such balanced treatments as those of J. I. Packer — tends to integrate the genuine insights of both sides. It affirms with the wisdom view that Scripture is the sufficient guide to God's moral will, that the anxious hunt for hidden signs is a snare, and that God honours and matures us through the responsible exercise of sanctified freedom; while affirming with the traditional view that God is a living and personal God who does providentially guide his children, who does give wisdom to those who ask, who does sometimes prompt and lead in ways that exceed mere deduction from principles, and whose peace does rightly attend the obedient choice. The upshot is a discernment of guidance that is Scripture-normed, wisdom-driven, prayerful, communal, and free — that seeks God's will primarily by becoming the kind of person, saturated in the Word and conformed to Christ, who will naturally and freely choose what pleases him, rather than by the decoding of oracles. This Evangelical wrestling with guidance is one of the tradition's most valuable contributions to the whole Church's discernment, for the guidance question is a universal one, and the Evangelical debate has clarified it as no other tradition's discussion has.

The perspicuity of Scripture and the priesthood of discernment

The Evangelical confidence that discernment is the birthright of every believer, and not the preserve of a clerical or scholarly elite, rests upon a doctrine inherited from the Reformation: the perspicuity, or clarity, of Scripture. The Reformers held, against the claim that the Bible was too obscure to be entrusted to the ordinary Christian and could be read safely only under the Church's authoritative interpretation, that the Scriptures are clear in all things necessary for salvation — that their central message is plain enough for the ploughboy to grasp, and that the Spirit who inspired the Word illumines the humble reader to understand it. From this flows the Evangelical conviction that every believer, indwelt by the Spirit and instructed in the Word, is competent and indeed obliged to discern for himself — to test what he is taught against the Scriptures, as the Bereans did, and not to surrender his conscience uncritically to any human authority. This is the priesthood of all believers extended to the discernment of truth, and it is one of the tradition's great and liberating insights, for it refuses to let the discernment of the people of God be confiscated by any elite and returns it to the whole Body.

Yet the Evangelical tradition, at its wisest, has recognised that the perspicuity of Scripture and the priesthood of the believer do not license a rootless individualism in which each reader is a law unto himself and every interpretation is as good as another. The clarity of Scripture pertains to what is necessary for salvation, not to every disputed question; the Spirit's illumination does not dispense with the labour of study, the teaching gifts God has given to the Church, or the accumulated wisdom of the communion of saints; and the individual believer discerns rightly not in isolation but within the fellowship of the Church, tested by and testing the community, under the ministry of teachers whom the same Spirit has given for the equipping of the saints. The mature Evangelical discernment thus holds together two truths that the careless set at odds: that every believer has the right and the duty to discern, and that no believer discerns alone — so that the priesthood of all believers is not the atomising of discernment into a million private judgements but its distribution through the whole Body, each member bringing his Spirit-given portion to the common testing of the truth under the sufficient and clear Word of God.

Chapter Thirty-One

Guidance and the Will of God

The most distinctive and instructive contribution of the Evangelical tradition to the whole Church's discernment is its long, vigorous, and clarifying debate over the question of guidance — how the individual believer is to discern the will of God for the concrete decisions of an ordinary life: whom to marry, what work to take up, where to live, which of two good paths to walk. Every tradition faces this question, but none has argued it out with the thoroughness of the Evangelicals, and the debate between the two great Evangelical positions has cast more light on the guidance question than any other discussion in Christendom. It is worth setting out with care, for the stakes are pastoral and immense: a whole generation of earnest believers has been either paralysed by one account of guidance or liberated by another, and the difference turns on a genuine question of discernment.

The traditional view: an individual blueprint

The first position, which may be called the traditional or specific-will view, holds that God has a detailed, individual plan for each believer's life — a specific will regarding vocation, marriage, location, and the rest — which the believer is responsible to discover and to follow, and outside of which he falls short of God's best. On this account the task of guidance is the discovery of a pre-existing divine blueprint, and God is understood to make it known through a convergence of indicators: the principles of Scripture, the leading felt in prayer, the inner witness or "peace" of the Spirit, the counsel of mature believers, the providential arrangement of circumstances into "open" and "closed" doors, and sometimes more direct inward promptings or impressions. The strength of this view, and the reason it has commanded such devotion, is its vivid sense of a personal God who cares about the details of his children's lives and who leads them individually; its appeal is to the God who numbers the hairs of our heads and orders the steps of the righteous, and who would surely not leave his children without direction in the great decisions of their lives.

The evangelical debate over guidance — whether God has a detailed individual blueprint to be uncovered, or grants a sanctified freedom to be exercised within his revealed will — is illumined by the Confucian vision of maturity as 從心所欲不踰矩, the freedom of the ripened heart that "follows its desires without transgressing the line." The wisdom view, rightly held, is precisely this: not a cramped hunt for a hidden plan but the liberty of a heart so formed by Scripture and the Spirit that its very desires may increasingly be trusted. The limit is the ground of that freedom — for the Christian it is not self-cultivation but the indwelling Spirit who conforms the desiring heart to the mind of Christ.

The wisdom view: Scripture, freedom, and sanctified wisdom

The second position, which may be called the wisdom view and which has been powerfully argued by such writers as Garry Friesen and Bruce Waltke, holds that the quest for a hidden individual blueprint is both unbiblical and spiritually harmful. God's moral will, it argues — his commands and principles for holy living — is revealed fully and sufficiently in Scripture, and this is the proper and only object of the believer's search for God's will; within the wide bounds of that moral will, God grants his children a real freedom to choose, and calls them to exercise it with sanctified wisdom — weighing the counsel of Scripture's principles, seeking godly advice, assessing circumstances soberly, and choosing, as free and maturing sons rather than anxious servants, what seems best for the glory of God. The wisdom view presses a searching critique of the specific-will account: that the endless hunt for a hidden, individual "centre" of God's will breeds paralysis in the timid, superstition in the credulous, and a kind of spiritualised fortune-telling that reads divine messages into coincidences; that it can become an evasion of the responsible freedom to which God calls the mature; and that its warrant in Scripture is surprisingly thin, since the biblical saints are far more often shown exercising wise, free, God-fearing judgement than decoding hidden signs. Where Scripture does depict direct guidance — a vision, a prophetic word, an angelic direction — it is God's sovereign initiative, not a technique the believer can trigger; the normal biblical pattern is the wise heart applying the revealed will of God to the open field of freedom.

The means and their misuse

Between these poles the ordinary believer must actually decide, and the debate has clarified how the various means of guidance genuinely function and how each may be misused. Scripture is the indispensable and sufficient ground, revealing the moral will within which every particular choice must fall; its misuse is the plucking of isolated verses as private oracles, the practice of opening the Bible at random for a message, which treats the Word as a divining rod rather than as the revelation of God's character and commands. Prayer is the seeking of a heart aligned with God; its misuse is the demand that God furnish an unmistakable inner sign before one will move. Counsel is the wisdom of the community, the safety found in many advisers; its misuse is the search for a counsellor who will ratify what one has already decided. Circumstances are the providential field of action; their misuse is the superstitious reading of every open or closed door as an infallible divine telegram, forgetting that an open door may be a temptation and a closed one a trial to be pressed through. And the peace of Christ, which Scripture bids us let rule as umpire in our hearts, is a real and precious confirmation of a rightly ordered choice; its misuse is to absolutise a feeling of peace that may be only the relief of having decided, or the false calm of presumption, or to mistake the absence of peace for prohibition when it is merely the natural fear that attends any costly obedience.

The mature integration

The mature Evangelical position, represented by such balanced teachers as J. I. Packer and Dallas Willard, does not simply choose one pole but integrates the genuine insights of both. It affirms with the wisdom view that Scripture is the sufficient guide to God's moral will, that the anxious hunt for hidden signs is a snare, and that God matures his children through the responsible exercise of a sanctified freedom; and it affirms with the traditional view that God is a living and personal God who really does guide his children, who gives wisdom to those who ask, who does sometimes prompt and lead in ways that exceed mere deduction from principles, and whose peace rightly attends the obedient choice. The upshot is a discernment of guidance that is Scripture-normed, wisdom-driven, prayerful, communal, and free — one that seeks God's will primarily by becoming the kind of person, saturated in the Word and conformed to Christ, who will naturally and freely choose what pleases God, rather than by the anxious decoding of oracles. Willard's image of a "conversational relationship" with God captures the balance: God does speak, and the mature believer learns his voice through long intimacy, but that voice is always tested against the written Word and the character of Christ and never set above them.

Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the Evangelical guidance debate is, at its root, a debate about how pneumatic discernment is — whether the guidance of God is a matter of natural wisdom applying a written text, or of the Spirit's living lead perceived by a heart conformed to Christ, or, as the mature view rightly sees, of both together. The tradition serves the whole Church best when it holds its magnificent devotion to the sufficiency of the Word together with the confession that the Word is spiritually discerned, so that guidance is neither a superstitious decoding of signs nor a merely prudential naturalism, but the free choice of a Spirit-renewed mind that has come, in the Word and in prayer, to want what God wants.

God guides most surely not by dropping signs in your path, but by making you the kind of person who, wanting what he wants, walks the right road freely.

Blueprint and wisdom: the two accounts of guidance, and the discernment between them

The evangelical debate over guidance turns on a distinction between three senses of "the will of God." His sovereign or decretive will is his hidden purpose, by which all things come to pass — known only after the event. His moral or preceptive will is his revealed command in Scripture — known, binding, and the same for all. The dispute concerns a supposed third: an individual will, a detailed personal blueprint — this job, this house, this spouse — which each believer must discover. The traditional or "blueprint" view holds that God has such a specific plan, and that the mark of the spiritual life is to find it, reading his guidance off inner impressions, open and closed doors, circumstantial signs, and a felt peace. The wisdom view — its ablest modern advocates being Garry Friesen and Bruce Waltke — answers that Scripture nowhere commands us to hunt a hidden individual blueprint: God reveals his moral will, and then, within its wide bounds, grants us freedom to choose by sanctified wisdom — the difference, in the familiar figure, between hunting an invisible "dot" and moving freely within a spacious "circle."

The choice between them is itself a matter of discernment, for each view has its characteristic corruption. The blueprint view, pressed too far, breeds paralysis — the anxious terror of "missing God's will" that freezes the soul before every ordinary decision; superstition — the reading of circumstances as omens, the laying of fleeces, the treating of a stray verse or an empty parking space as an oracle; abdication — the use of "God told me" to escape the labour of wisdom and the accountability of counsel; and manipulation — the weaponising of "the Lord has shown me" to bind another's freedom. The wisdom view has its own opposite peril: a brisk rationalism that, in banishing the fleece, can quench the Spirit's genuine and gentle promptings and reduce guidance to prudence alone. The book's own path runs between — Scripture's moral will as the fixed and sufficient norm; within it, freedom exercised through sanctified wisdom, godly counsel, and open eyes; and the real but non-coercive promptings of the Spirit, always tested by the Word and never usurping its place, with peace received as a confirmation and never consulted as an oracle.

In practice this yields not a technique for extracting certainty but a posture: gather wisdom, take counsel, weigh the circumstances, pray for and welcome the Spirit's nudge, and then — freed from the tyranny of the hidden dot — choose, trusting the sovereign God to govern what he has not disclosed. The Confucian sages knew the peace of just such a posture. The Doctrine of the Mean contrasts two men: 居易以俟命 (jū yì yǐ sì mìng), "the gentleman dwells at ease and awaits what is decreed, while the mean man walks in peril, hoping for lucky chances" (Zhongyong 14). The parallel is close — the discerning soul rests in its freedom and does not scrabble after omens; yet the Christian awaits not an impersonal decree but the providence of a Father, and dwells at ease not in fatalism but in trust.

Chapter Thirty-Two

Discernment, Doctrine, and the Renewed Mind

Alongside the guidance of the individual life, the Evangelical tradition has made the discernment of truth — the testing of teaching and teachers against the Word of God — its most characteristic and vigilant exercise. For the Evangelical, the paradigmatic act of discernment is Berean: the reception of teaching with all readiness of mind, joined to the daily searching of the Scriptures to see whether the things taught are so. This chapter treats that doctrinal discernment, the renewed mind that alone can perform it, and the characteristic dangers into which the vigilant can fall.

The Berean testing of teaching

The Evangelical tradition takes with full seriousness the apostolic commands to test the spirits, to prove all things, to hold fast the sound pattern of teaching, and to reject even an angel from heaven who should preach another gospel. It produces, in consequence, a tradition marked by a vigilant concern for sound doctrine and a readiness to weigh teachers and teachings against Scripture, holding that a claimed revelation, prophecy, or leading that contradicts the plain teaching of the Word is by that fact alone not from God. The scriptural marks of false teaching are well known to the tradition and are drawn directly from the apostolic warnings: the denial or dilution of the person and work of Christ, which is the Johannine test; the pursuit of gain and the exploitation of the flock; a manner of life that contradicts the profession; the sowing of division; and the introduction of novelties that depart from the faith once for all delivered to the saints. This testing of teaching is a precious and necessary service, and the Evangelical vigilance for the purity of the gospel has again and again preserved the Church from corruption.

The renewed mind and the illumination of the Spirit

Yet the Evangelical tradition knows, at its best, that this testing is not the cold work of a natural intelligence sifting propositions, for Scripture is rightly understood only by a mind renewed and illumined by the Spirit. The tradition takes seriously the noetic effects of sin — the corruption of the understanding itself, so that the natural mind is not a neutral instrument but a darkened one, prone to suppress the truth and to rationalise its own desires — and it insists therefore that genuine discernment requires the renewing of the mind of which the Apostle speaks, the transformation by which the believer is enabled to prove and approve the will of God, and the illumination of the Spirit, by which the same Spirit who inspired the Word opens the believer's understanding to receive it. The Word is the objective standard, but only the renewed and Spirit-illumined mind can rightly apply it; and so the tradition joins to its emphasis on doctrine an emphasis on sanctification, on the cultivation of a mind and heart conformed to Christ, as the personal precondition of sound discernment. This is also the ground of the Evangelical confidence that discernment is the birthright of every believer and not the preserve of an elite — the priesthood of all believers extended to the discernment of truth, since every Spirit-indwelt Christian has, in the measure of his renewal, the mind of Christ.

The discernment ministries and their dangers

The Evangelical zeal for doctrinal purity has given rise, especially in the modern era, to dedicated "discernment ministries" devoted to the testing and exposure of error, and their proper use and characteristic dangers together form an important case study in the discernment of the discerners. At their best such ministries perform a genuine service, warning the flock against real wolves and defending the gospel against real corruption. But the tradition's own wisdom, and the whole grid of criteria this book has traced, exposes their besetting temptation: that the vigilance for truth curdles into a censorious, suspicious, and loveless spirit — a heresy-hunting that delights in the fall of others, that assumes the worst, that magnifies secondary differences into tests of fellowship, and that mistakes its own contentiousness for faithfulness. This is a counterfeit of discernment, and it is exposed by the very criteria it neglects: for the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, and gentleness, and a "discernment" that produces pride, division, and contempt is by that fruit revealed as fleshly, whatever the truth of the propositions it defends. The Apostle who commanded the testing of the spirits also declared that knowledge without love is nothing, and that one may possess all knowledge and be, without love, a mere clanging cymbal.

Love as the context of discernment

The mature Evangelical teachers have therefore insisted that doctrinal discernment must be exercised within, and never apart from, the context of love. Discernment is a service of the truth, and the truth is served in love or it is betrayed; the aim of testing teaching is not the vindication of the tester but the protection and building-up of the Body and the recovery of the erring. This is the balance that the great Evangelical teachers of discernment have sought to hold — a vigilance for truth that never becomes a contempt for persons, a firmness in the faith that is clothed in gentleness, a testing of teaching that is itself tested by love. Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the Evangelical discernment of doctrine is a genuine and necessary exercise of the pneumatic gift — the renewed mind, illumined by the Spirit, perceiving the truth and falsehood of what is taught — but it stands under the same measure it applies, for the surest sign that doctrinal vigilance is truly of the Spirit is the love and humility in which it is held, and the surest sign that it is not is the pride and the loveless censoriousness that so easily counterfeit it.

Test every teaching; but test your testing too — for the heresy-hunter and the heretic can share the one sin of a loveless heart.

The indigenous Chinese witness: the discernment of spirit from soul

Before we set the Evangelical discernment beside its classical Chinese parallel, a tradition must be honoured that stands, remarkably, at the meeting-point of the two: the indigenous Chinese Protestantism of the twentieth century, and above all the three theologians Watchman Nee (倪柝聲), Witness Lee (李常受), and Wang Mingdao (王明道), who between them worked out a pneumatology of the human person that makes the discernment of spirit from soul the very centre of the Christian life. Their achievement is of peculiar moment for this book, for they took the Pauline anthropology that underlies our whole governing text — the distinction of the psychikos, the soulish or natural person, from the pneumatikos, the spiritual — and developed it, out of the crucible of a suffering Chinese church, into a detailed and pastorally exacting science of the interior life. Reading Scripture in three languages and formed in a tradition that had never separated knowing from participation, they grasped with unusual clarity that the fundamental discernment is the discernment of what proceeds from the human spirit, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, from what proceeds from the soul — the seat of the natural mind, emotion, and will — and that the whole peril of the spiritual life lies in the soul's genius for counterfeiting the spirit. It is a striking testimony to the truth this study contends for that these Chinese Christians arrived, independently, at the very axiom of our Prolegomenon, which their own tradition expressed in three characters — 靈先於存在, "spirit precedes existence": pneumatology before ontology.

Watchman Nee and the three functions of the spirit

Watchman Nee, distilling twenty years of itinerant ministry across China into his great work on the spiritual man, gave the tradition its architectural centre: the teaching that the human person is spirit, soul, and body (靈, 魂, 體), and that the human spirit — the innermost part, the organ of contact with God — functions through three integrated operations, each of which is an instrument of discernment. The first is intuition (直覺, zhíjué), the spirit's own direct, non-discursive knowing — a perception that does not reason its way to its object but receives it, as a light switched on in a dark room does not argue the furniture into being but simply reveals what was always there. This intuition, Nee taught, is the faculty by which the revelations of God and the movements of the Holy Spirit are known to the believer; the mind may afterward help us to understand what has been shown, but the knowing itself arises in the spirit, immediately, beneath and before all reasoning. And Nee grounds this precisely in the tenth to twelfth verses of the second chapter of First Corinthians — the same passage that governs this whole book — noting even that the verb Paul uses for the Spirit's knowing of the things of God is the verb of direct, immediate perception rather than of gradual, accumulative acquaintance: the spirit's knowing is the knowing of sight, not of inference.

The second function is conscience (良心, liángxīn), which Nee understood not merely as the negative prohibitor of wrongdoing but as the positive moral organ of the spirit, the faculty that registers the moral significance of what intuition has perceived and co-witnesses with the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says his conscience bears him witness in the Spirit. The third is fellowship or communion (交通, jiāotōng, the Chinese rendering of koinōnia) — the sustained participatory communion with God that is not a passing event but the abiding relational field within which intuition and conscience operate, so that the spirit discerns rightly only insofar as it dwells in unbroken communion with the Spirit of God. But Nee's most valuable contribution to the discernment of spirits is a pastoral warning of great precision, and it is one this book has met in every tradition: that the genuine intuition of the spirit is quiet and slight, not clamorous or overwhelming, and that the soul's strong emotions must never be mistaken for the spirit's still perception. God does not, Nee insisted, cast the believer to the ground by an irresistible force or speak thunderously from heaven, but works quietly in the spirit to impress his mind upon the intuition; and the confusion of the soul's emotional intensity with the spirit's quiet knowing — the very error to which an undiscerning enthusiasm is most prone — is among the commonest and most dangerous failures of discernment. Here Nee gives the psychikos and the pneumatikos of First Corinthians a razor's edge: the soulish counterfeit is loud, and the spiritual reality is quiet, and the whole art is to tell the one from the other. To this end Nee taught the necessity of the breaking of the outer man — the disciplined, often painful reduction of the soul's self-assertive strength, that the imprisoned spirit might be released to function freely; for the strong and unbroken soul, however religious, overwhelms the quiet spirit and makes true discernment impossible.

Witness Lee and the mingled spirit

The soulish counterfeit is loud; the spiritual reality is quiet — and the whole art is to tell the one from the other.

Witness Lee, Nee's foremost co-worker, carried this anthropology to its pneumatological ground in the doctrine of the mingled spirit (調和的靈), built upon the Apostle's declaration that "he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit" with him. The regenerate human spirit, Lee taught, is joined and mingled with the indwelling Holy Spirit to become a single operative reality — not confounded, so that the Creator-creature distinction is abolished, nor merely juxtaposed, but genuinely mingled, the divine and the human spirit functioning together as one — and it is by this mingled spirit that the believer knows, discerns, and lives. Discernment, on this understanding, is the operation of the human spirit indwelt and empowered by the divine, and the whole of the Christian life is the progressive expansion of the mingled spirit's governance over the soul and body — the psychical yielded, degree by degree, to the pneumatological, until, in the eschaton, the soulish body (the sōma psychikon of First Corinthians) is raised a spiritual body (the sōma pneumatikon), the human person wholly permeated by and one with the divine Spirit. Every spiritual discipline — the intake of the Word, prayer, fasting, silence, confession, worship, and fellowship — is, in Lee's vision, a means of this progressive densification of the Spirit's presence and the corresponding lessening of the natural self's resistance; and the discernment of the mingled spirit grows as the disciplines do their work. Lee guards the doctrine carefully against pantheism — to be one spirit with the Lord is to participate in the divine Spirit-life, not to be absorbed into the divine essence — and in doing so he states, in his own key, the very distinction this book has drawn between the Christian participation in the personal Spirit and the impersonal merging of the mystical traditions that lack him.

Wang Mingdao and the sincerity of the heart

Wang Mingdao, the great independent pastor of Beijing, contributed to this tradition the moral and penitential dimension without which the pneumatology of spirit and soul would be a mere psychology. His central concern was the sincerity of the heart — the question he would press upon his hearers, whether their hearts were genuinely sincere before God or secretly divided — and he made repentance (悔改, the Chinese metanoia) not a preliminary to the spiritual life but its constitutive and recurring dynamic. Wang taught, in effect, a repentance cycle that is at the same time a cycle of discernment: communion with God brings light; the light brings exposure, in which the conscience registers what the light has revealed of the divided heart; exposure brings grief and true repentance; repentance brings restoration; and restoration opens into a deeper communion, from which the cycle begins again at a greater depth. The pivotal moment is the exposure, and it is precisely the work of the virtue-conscience — the spirit's moral organ turning the light of God upon the self and discerning, without flattery, the actual condition of the heart. This is the discernment of the self, the hardest of all the objects of discernment, made the daily discipline of the ordinary believer; and Wang's insistence that the sincerity of the heart is the precondition of all true spiritual knowing coheres exactly with the desert's teaching that purity of heart is the ground of discernment, and with our governing text's warning that the natural man cannot receive the things of the Spirit.

And Wang Mingdao's theology was written, at the last, not only in his words but in his body, for his teaching on the sincerity of the heart was tested in the most terrible form the century could devise. Imprisoned for more than two decades for his refusal to compromise the independence of the church, Wang passed through his own agonising enactment of the cycle he had preached — including a failure under interrogation, a recantation wrung from a divided heart, and then the exposure, the grief, the repentance, and the long restoration that followed — so that his life became, as his interpreters have said, not an addendum to his theology but its living exegesis. In him the discernment of the sincere heart ceased to be a doctrine and became a martyrdom of the interior life, the costliest possible demonstration that the exposure of the divided heart to the light of God is the narrow gate through which alone the soul comes to a knowing that is true. Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the three Chinese theologians together render one of the most valuable of all modern accounts of the pneumatic discernment this book has traced: they locate discernment in the human spirit indwelt and mingled with the Holy Spirit; they distinguish, with unmatched precision, the quiet perception of the spirit from the loud counterfeit of the soul; and they root the whole in the sincerity of a heart daily exposed, by conscience, to the light of God — a witness the more compelling for having been sealed, in Wang Mingdao, with the sufferings of a confessor. It is fitting that a tradition which so grasped the pneumatic ground should have expressed, in its own tongue, the very axiom of this study — that the spirit precedes existence, and that to discern is, first and last, to know by the Spirit.

The latent power of the soul: Watchman Nee and the counterfeit of the spiritual

Watchman Nee (倪柝聲) gave the Chinese Church — and through it the worldwide evangelical world — the most rigorous popular anatomy of the tripartite person: 靈 (líng, spirit), 魂 (hún, soul), and 體 (tǐ, body). The spirit, he taught, is the organ of communion with God, bearing three functions — 直覺 (zhíjué, intuition, the spirit's direct knowing), 良心 (liángxīn, conscience), and 交通 (jiāotōng, communion or fellowship); the soul is the seat of mind, emotion, and will, the natural self. And on the razor-line between them Nee laid the whole labour of discernment, for the peril of the spiritual life is that the soulish (ψυχικός, psychikos) forever counterfeits the spiritual (πνευματικός, pneumatikos): brilliant thought, surging emotion, and strong will can all masquerade as the moving of the Spirit. "The word of God is living... piercing to the division of soul and of spirit" (Heb 4:12): to discern is, first of all, to tell the spirit's promptings from the soul's.

Nee's most original and unsettling contribution to discernment was his doctrine of the latent power of the soul — the buried psychic force of the unfallen Adam, now fallen and, he warned, exploitable by the enemy. Phenomena that dazzle — telepathy, clairvoyance, healings, mighty displays of will — need not be from God at all; they may be the soul's own latent power, the very stuff of the occult and of the false religions, costuming itself as the Spirit. Here Nee names, out of a Chinese context with its living traditions of psychic and folk-religious power, a counterfeit the Western Church too easily overlooks: not every wonder is the Holy Spirit, for the soul and the powers have wonders of their own. The classical Chinese anthropology had itself divided the self into 魂魄 (hún pò), the cloud-soul that ascends and the white-soul bound to earth; Nee seized the native vocabulary but drove a deeper wedge — between the whole natural man, cloud-soul and all, and the spirit reborn by the Holy Spirit, so that the discernment he demands is not between two souls but between the self, however refined, and the Spirit of God.

The remedy Nee prescribed was the breaking of the outer man — the disciplined mortification of the soulish self so that the spirit may be released and its intuition made clear; discernment, for Nee, is impossible to an unbroken soul, whose own noise drowns the still voice of the spirit. Witness Lee (李常受) carried the anatomy toward union in his teaching of the 調和的靈 (tiáohé de líng), the mingled spirit — the human spirit joined to the Holy Spirit as the single organ of discernment and life. And Wang Mingdao (王明道), martyr-confessor of integrity, set against all counterfeit the plumb-line of 誠 (chéng), sincerity — the whole-life truthfulness without which the finest spiritual profession is hollow. Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the Chinese evangelical witness gives the tradition its sharpest name for the master-counterfeit — the soulish that apes the spiritual, kin to the Orthodox prelest, to the psychikos of Saint Paul, to the angel of light — and its sharpest remedy: a broken and sincere heart in which the reborn spirit, mingled with God's Spirit, can at last discern.

The Chinese parallel: timely wisdom and the weighing of the mean

The Evangelical debate over guidance — and in particular the wisdom-view's contention that God grants his children, within the bounds of his revealed moral will, a real freedom to be exercised by a sanctified practical wisdom rather than by the anxious decoding of signs — finds a close and clarifying counterpart in the Confucian ideal of timely wisdom. The Doctrine of the Mean praises the noble person who hits the mean appropriate to each moment (時中, shí zhōng, "timeliness"), neither rigidly applying a rule regardless of circumstance nor abandoning principle to expediency, but discerning, with a cultivated judgement, what the particular situation requires; and the Confucian tradition names this adaptive discernment 權 (quán), the "weighing" by which the wise man bends the application of a principle to the shape of the concrete case without betraying the principle itself. This is, almost exactly, the wisdom-view's account of guidance: not the mechanical following of a rule nor the superstitious reading of omens, but the free exercise of a Word-formed, Spirit-renewed practical wisdom that weighs the concrete circumstance and chooses well. The Berean testing of teaching, likewise, corresponds to the Confucian reverence-yet-testing of received doctrine, the "knowing of words" by which the disciple weighs even the teaching of his masters against the pattern of the Way.

The parallel is genuine and the convergence real, for both traditions distrust the anxious rule-seeker and prize the cultivated judgement that discerns the fitting act in the fluid particular. Yet the ground of the weighing differs at the root: the Confucian weighs by the heart-mind cultivated toward the pattern of Heaven, an impersonal order to be conformed to; the Evangelical weighs by the Word of a personal God and the renewing of the mind by his Spirit, so that the freedom he exercises is the freedom of a son before a Father who guides him, and not merely the poise of a sage attuned to an impersonal mean.

Weighed by the pneumatological measure

Weighed by the measure, the Evangelical tradition affirms the pneumatic ground at its best — in its doctrine of the renewed mind, the Spirit's illumination, and the spiritual person who discerns what the natural cannot — but it is the tradition most liable, in its weaker forms, to let that ground slip. Where a strong bibliocentrism combines with an inherited common-sense rationalism, discernment can flatten into the merely natural work of testing propositions against texts; and the wisdom view of guidance, right as it is to deflate a superstitious hunt for signs, can overcorrect into a prudential naturalism that quietly forgets the Spirit's living lead — as if discernment were sanctified cleverness rather than the pneumatic perception of the mind of Christ. The guidance debate, seen from the Prolegomenon, is at bottom a debate about how pneumatic discernment is; and the Evangelical tradition serves the whole Church best when it holds its magnificent devotion to the Word together with the confession that the Word is spiritually discerned, so that the letter and the Spirit are never divided.

In Wang Mingdao the discernment of the sincere heart ceased to be a doctrine and became a martyrdom of the interior life.

然

Part Nine

The Charismatic and Pentecostal Traditions

The Spirit still speaks — the charism of discerning of spirits, the weighing of prophecy, and a Pentecostal theology of discernment.

Chapter Thirty-Three

The Charism, the Weighing of Prophecy, and the Pentecostal Discernment

The Charismatic and Pentecostal traditions bring to the discernment of spirits a distinctive and indispensable conviction: that the gifts of the Holy Spirit described in the New Testament, including prophecy, tongues, healing, and the discerning of spirits itself, remain available to and operative in the Church today, and that discernment is therefore not merely the testing of doctrine and the reading of providence but an active, Spirit-given capacity to perceive the spiritual realities at work in a person, a situation, or an assembly. This conviction, born at the Azusa Street revival in 1906 and spread through the classical Pentecostal denominations, the mid-century charismatic renewal that touched every historic communion, and the "Third Wave" of more recent decades, restores the diakrisis pneumatōn of First Corinthians to the centre of the Church's life as a living operation rather than a historical relic. But the same traditions have had to learn — often through painful experience — that the recovery of the Spirit's gifts makes the discipline of testing more necessary, not less; for where prophecy is exercised, prophecy must be weighed, and where the Spirit is expected to move, the counterfeit and the merely human must be discerned from the genuine with special care. This chapter introduces the charismatic and Pentecostal discernment and its characteristic disciplines and dangers, and the chapters that complete this Part will unfold them in full.

The charism of discerning of spirits

The gift of the discerning of spirits, listed by Paul among the manifestations of the Spirit given for the common good, is understood in these traditions as a Spirit-given ability to perceive the source and character of a spiritual manifestation — to discern whether a given prompting, prophecy, manifestation, or influence proceeds from the Holy Spirit, from the human spirit, or from an evil spirit. It is exercised with particular seriousness in the ministry of deliverance, where the discernment of the demonic from the psychological and the merely fleshly is a matter of grave pastoral responsibility, and where the traditions at their most mature have learned to proceed with great care, humility, and sobriety, resisting both the credulous tendency to attribute every affliction to demons and the sceptical tendency to deny the reality of the demonic altogether. The genuine exercise of this charism, the responsible teachers of these traditions insist, is not a spectacular power to be paraded but a humble gift to be exercised in submission to Scripture, in the fellowship and under the testing of the Church, and in the service of love — and it is subject, like every charism, to the whole grid of criteria we set out in Part One, above all the christological test, the fruit-test, and the mark of humility. A "discernment" that is censorious, self-exalting, divisive, or unaccountable is, whatever it claims, not the genuine gift, for the Spirit's gifts build up the Body in love.

The weighing of prophecy

The most important discernment discipline of these traditions, and the one with the widest significance for the whole Church, is the weighing of prophecy. Paul's instruction is explicit and it is foundational: let the prophets speak, and let the others weigh — diakrinetōsan, let them discern — what is said. Prophecy, in the New Testament and in the responsible charismatic understanding, is not to be received uncritically as the very oracle of God, on the level of Scripture; it is to be tested, sifted, and weighed by the assembly and its leaders, held always to the norm of Scripture and the character of Christ, and received only in the measure that it passes the test. This principle has been given careful and influential — though also contested — theological form by Wayne Grudem, whose study The Gift of Prophecy in the New Testament and Today argues that New Testament congregational prophecy, as distinct from the inscripturated words of the canonical prophets and apostles, is a Spirit-prompted but fallible human report of something God brings to mind, which is precisely why it must always be weighed and never simply obeyed, and which can therefore contain a mixture of the genuine and the merely human. Whether or not one accepts every detail of Grudem's account — and it remains debated among Pentecostal and Reformed scholars alike — the underlying discipline is the sure teaching of the whole tradition: prophecy is subordinate to Scripture, prophecy must be weighed, and the assembly that receives prophecy without testing it has abandoned the very discipline the apostle commanded. The history of the charismatic movement, with its recurrent episodes of prophetic excess and failure — from the controversies over particular prophetic movements to the debated revivalist phenomena of recent decades — is in large part a history of the consequences of neglecting, and then painfully recovering, this apostolic discipline of weighing.

Toward a Pentecostal theology of discernment

The Pentecostal tradition has, in recent decades, produced serious scholarship that raises its practical discernment to the level of a developed theology, and two figures deserve particular notice. Gordon Fee, the great Pentecostal New Testament scholar, in his magisterial study of the Spirit in Paul, God's Empowering Presence, provided the tradition with a rigorous, Scripture-normed pneumatology that grounds the gifts, including discernment, in careful exegesis and holds them firmly to their apostolic shape and purpose — the building up of the Body in love under the lordship of Christ. And Amos Yong, perhaps the most significant Pentecostal theologian of discernment, in works such as Discerning the Spirit(s) and Spirit-Word-Community, has articulated a comprehensive theological hermeneutic of discernment in which the testing of the spirits is understood as a fundamental and pervasively Christian act, exercised by attending together to Spirit, Word, and Community — the three interwoven norms by which the Church discerns what is and is not of God. For Yong, discernment is not merely the propositional testing of doctrine but a Spirit-enabled perception of the divine presence and activity in the world, disciplined always by the Word and exercised always in and by the community, so that Scripture, the Spirit's living illumination, and the communal testing of the Body function together as a threefold cord that cannot easily be broken. This Pentecostal-ecumenical theology of discernment, which self-consciously seeks to integrate the insights of the whole Church, points directly toward the synthesis this book will attempt in its final Part; for it recovers, in a contemporary and rigorously theological form, the ancient truth that discernment is the work of the Spirit, under the Word, in the community — the very grammar that, this book contends, the whole Church holds in common.

Tongues, interpretation, and the ordering of the gifts

The Charismatic and Pentecostal traditions have had to exercise discernment not only upon prophecy but upon the whole range of the manifestational gifts, and nowhere more delicately than in the matter of tongues and their interpretation, which stand at the centre of the Apostle's own most sustained instruction on the ordering of the Spirit's gifts. In the fourteenth chapter of First Corinthians, Paul addresses a congregation whose enthusiasm for the spectacular gift of tongues had outrun its discernment, and he brings to bear a principle of the first importance: that the gifts of the Spirit are given for the edification of the Body, and are therefore to be governed, ordered, and weighed by that end. Tongues spoken in the assembly without interpretation, he teaches, edify no one but the speaker and leave the others unbuilt; they must therefore be interpreted, that the whole body may share in their meaning, and where there is no interpreter the speaker is to keep silence in the church. The discernment here is subtle and characteristically Pauline: the Apostle neither forbids the gift, as the fearful would, nor exalts it above its purpose, as the enthusiasts did, but orders it to the good of the Body — for God, he declares in a phrase that governs the whole of charismatic discernment, is not a God of confusion but of peace.

This Pauline ordering yields a criterion of discernment that reaches far beyond the particular question of tongues: that the genuine work of the Spirit builds up the Body in love and makes for order rather than confusion, while the counterfeit — whether it be a fleshly enthusiasm, a self-displaying spirituality, or a genuine gift wrenched from its proper end — makes for disorder, division, and the exaltation of the individual over the community. Let all things be done for edification, the Apostle commands, and let all things be done decently and in order; and the charismatic tradition, at its most mature, has discerned its own life by this measure, welcoming the Spirit's gifts with open hands while ordering them, weighing them, and subordinating even the most dramatic of them to the upbuilding of the Body in love. The same First Corinthians that most exalts the gifts places between its two chapters on them the great hymn to love, and thereby teaches the deepest discernment of all: that the gifts without love are nothing, that love is the more excellent way, and that the surest sign of the Spirit in any manifestation is not its power or its strangeness but the love that it serves and the peace that it builds.

The self-silencing of the Church: cessationism weighed

No question so divides the modern church on the discernment of the Spirit as whether the Spirit still gives what he gave at Pentecost. The cessationist answers no — at least for the revelatory and sign gifts of prophecy, tongues, healing, and miracle — holding that these belonged to the foundational age of the apostles, served to authenticate the giving of revelation, and ceased when that revelation was complete and its canon closed. The position is held by learned and godly men, and it must be stated at its strongest before it is weighed: it springs from a right zeal for the sufficiency of Scripture and a right horror at the manifest abuses of the gifts, and it can marshal the argument, framed most formidably by B. B. Warfield in Counterfeit Miracles, that the miraculous clustered about the apostles precisely because its office was to accredit them and their word.

And yet this book must say plainly that cessationism is, in its effect, among the gravest failures of discernment the Western church has ever committed — a doctrine that, meaning to guard the Word, has silenced the Spirit, and has taught the people of God to disbelieve in the very power they are promised. It is 畫地為牢 (huà dì wéi láo), the drawing of a circle upon the ground and the calling of it a prison: a confinement wholly self-imposed, ruling out in advance what God has nowhere ruled out, and shutting the Church within a boundary of its own chalk. For the Spirit "blows where it wills" (John 3:8), and the Lord who is "the same yesterday and today and for ever" (Hebrews 13:8) has signed no decree of his own retirement.

Cessationism draws a circle on the ground and calls it the will of God.

The perfect that is to come: the exegesis examined

The doctrine rests, exegetically, upon a slender and much-strained foundation, and chiefly upon a single misread verse. "When the perfect comes," Paul writes, "the partial passes away" (1 Corinthians 13:10), and the cessationist takes "the perfect" (to teleion) to mean the completed canon of Scripture, so that prophecy and its kindred fell silent when the last book was penned. But Paul says in the very next breath what he means: "now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face; now I know in part, then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known" (v. 12) — and "face to face," the beatific vision, is the End, and not the bound volume of the New Testament. The gifts are "in part" not until the canon closes but until the Parousia, when faith gives way to sight. To make "the perfect" the canon is 郢書燕說 (yǐng shū yàn shuō), the reading into a text of a meaning its author never put there — the minister of Yan construing by candlelight a word that had slipped into the letter by accident. And no other text mends the breach, for Scripture nowhere announces the cessation of any gift, while Paul commands the contrary: "earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" (14:1), and "do not forbid speaking in tongues" (14:39).

Nor will the argument from authentication carry the weight laid upon it. The gifts did indeed accredit the apostles; but Paul grounds them, across 1 Corinthians 12 to 14, not chiefly in authentication but in the edification of the Body — "to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good" (12:7) — a purpose as needful in the twenty-first century as in the first. And he sets the gifts to run "until we all attain to the unity of the faith and... mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ" (Ephesians 4:13) — a goal the Church has plainly not yet reached. The burden of proof lies wholly upon the one who would silence what Scripture commands us to desire; and that burden has never once been discharged.

Scripture nowhere announces the cessation of any gift — and commands us to desire the very gifts cessationism forbids.

The witness of history, and the fruit of the doctrine

The witness of history compounds the cessationist's difficulty, for the gifts never in fact wholly ceased. Irenaeus and Tertullian attest prophecy and healing in the second century; the desert and the lives of the saints are thronged with the miraculous; the stream of gift and wonder runs, however unevenly, through every Christian century down to the Pentecostal outpouring of our own age. The cessationist must therefore either deny this vast testimony or explain it all away as delusion or fraud — and, doing so, he keeps watch like the farmer of the parable, 守株待兔 (shǒu zhū dài tù), guarding the stump and waiting for the hare, having fixed the whole outpouring of the Spirit to a single founding moment now past. But Pentecost was no stump; it was a spring, and its promise was pronounced "to you and to your children and to all who are far off, as many as the Lord our God shall call" (Acts 2:39) — the whole age of the Church, and not a marvel sealed in the first century.

What, then, is the fruit of the doctrine? It is the quenching of the Spirit that Paul forbids in the very breath in which he commands the testing of prophecy — "do not quench the Spirit, do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21) — and here is the deception's peculiar cunning: that it takes the abuses of the gifts as its warrant to renounce the gifts, which is 因噎廢食 (yīn yē fèi shí), the giving up of food for fear of choking. The glutton's cure for choking is not starvation but learning to eat; and the Spirit's cure for abused prophecy is not silence but discernment — the whole burden of this book. For the answer to the enthusiast's credulity was never the cessationist's unbelief, but the discerning heart that receives the gift and weighs it, holding fast the good and refusing the counterfeit. Cessationism and enthusiasm are not opposites but twin failures of the one discernment: the one accepts everything untested, the other rejects everything untried, and both are spared the harder labour of weighing. Weighed by the pneumatological measure, the doctrine that the Spirit has withdrawn his gifts is convicted of the very fault it fears — a failure to discern the living God, mistaking his continued speech for silence, and teaching the Church to say of the Pentecostal fire, "it is not the Lord," when it is.

The answer to the enthusiast’s credulity was never the cessationist’s unbelief, but the discerning heart that receives the gift and weighs it.

Chapter Thirty-Four

The Charism of Discerning of Spirits

The Charismatic and Pentecostal traditions restore to the centre of the Church's life the conviction that the discerning of spirits named by the Apostle is not a historical relic but a living gift, a present operation of the Spirit by which the Church perceives the spiritual realities at work in a person, a situation, or an assembly. This chapter treats that gift in itself: its scriptural nature, its exercise in the grave pastoral work of deliverance, and its subjection, like every charism, to the whole grid of criteria the Church has always applied.

The nature of the gift

The gift of the discerning of spirits, listed among the manifestations of the Spirit given for the common good, is understood in these traditions as a Spirit-given ability to perceive the source and character of a spiritual manifestation — to discern whether a given prompting, prophecy, manifestation, or influence proceeds from the Holy Spirit, from the human spirit, or from an evil spirit. It is not the same as natural insight into character, though the two may accompany one another; it is a supernatural perception, a gift, given as the Spirit wills and not to all, by which the spiritual sources at work in a situation are laid bare to the one who discerns. The traditions that have kept this gift alive have learned that it is exercised most seriously precisely where the stakes are highest — in the testing of prophecy, in the assessment of teaching and ministry, and above all in the ministry of deliverance — and that its genuine exercise is always humble, always submitted to Scripture and to the fellowship of the Church, and always in the service of love and the building-up of the Body.

Even the discerning of spirits — the charism of perceiving the unseen powers at work in a person or a place — is not without its sober Confucian shadow, for Confucius bade his disciples "respect the spirits but keep them at a distance" (敬鬼神而遠之), a wariness of the invisible realm that refused both credulous fascination and flat denial. The gospel does not keep the spirits at a distance but confronts and casts them out; yet it shares the sage's refusal of a morbid preoccupation with the demonic — for to hunt for devils in every shadow is itself a snare of the enemy, and a discernment grown lurid has already ceased to be sober.

The gift in the ministry of deliverance

The discerning of spirits is exercised with peculiar gravity in the ministry of deliverance, where the discernment of the demonic from the psychological and the merely fleshly is a matter of the most serious pastoral responsibility, and where the traditions at their most mature have learned to proceed with great care, humility, and sobriety. Here the tradition must hold together two truths and avoid two opposite errors. The first truth is that the demonic is real — that the New Testament everywhere assumes it, that the Lord himself cast out evil spirits, and that to deny the reality of the demonic altogether is to depart from the plain witness of Scripture and to leave the afflicted without a remedy. The second truth is that not every affliction is demonic — that most suffering is bodily, psychological, or circumstantial, and that to see a demon behind every illness, every sin, and every sorrow is a credulous and dangerous error that has done great harm, subjecting the sick to fruitless exorcisms and the depressed to a spiritual blame that deepens their despair. Between the credulous demonology that sees a demon everywhere and the sceptical rationalism that sees one nowhere, the mature tradition walks a careful path, exercising the gift of discernment with humility, collaborating readily with medical and psychological care, and holding as a decisive mark that genuine deliverance glorifies Christ, restores the afflicted to freedom and to their right mind, and never enslaves them to a perpetual deliverance-industry that feeds on fear.

The gift under the whole grid of criteria

The responsible teachers of these traditions insist that the charism of discerning of spirits, like every charism, is subject to the whole grid of criteria that this book has traced, and is emphatically not a self-authenticating power that places its possessor above testing. The gift is subject, first, to the christological test: the Spirit who gives it glorifies the incarnate Christ, and a "discernment" that dishonours Christ or departs from the apostolic faith is by that fact false. It is subject to the fruit test: the genuine gift builds up the Body in love and produces the fruit of the Spirit, while a "discernment" that is censorious, self-exalting, divisive, or unaccountable is, whatever it claims, not the genuine gift.
